sens: To make a hole or excavation by progressively pushing into the ground or stone
To deepen something in a literal sense, to make it deeper
To establish a solid foundation by digging down to the rock
G0900.detail:
1. The verb βαθύνω describes the action of digging, of pushing a tool or force into the ground to widen or deepen a space. It is the work of the excavator or builder who gradually removes the earth.
2. Generally, the word means to make something deeper. It is the act of digging down, sinking ever further.
3. In Luke 6:48, the word appears in Jesus' parable about the two houses. The wise man "digs deep" to lay the foundation on solid rock, instead of building on sand. Digging deep means making the extra effort to reach the rocky base, despite the work it requires. This action prepares a house capable of withstanding floods: it is an image of the solidity brought by conscientious work.
G0900.origine: The verb comes from the adjective βαθύς, which means "deep" (an ancient Indo-European root). The word describes the action of making deep, of deepening. In Hebrew, it sometimes translates the verb עמד (to stand, to persist), used in the Psalms to describe God's deep thoughts that "stand firm." The common idea is that of something being established solidly, going to the depths of things.
G0900.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:48. Jesus uses it to illustrate the solid foundation of a house in the face of trials. The man who hears Jesus' word and puts it into practice is compared to one who digs deep to build on the rock. It is a deliberate, meticulous act that requires courage and perseverance. The word emphasizes that spiritual solidity is not superficial: it requires deep work.
G0900.portee: This parable invites the reader to examine the foundations of their own spiritual life. Digging deep means not settling for a surface faith, but sinking one's roots into the Word of God and obedience to the very core of one's being. Jesus suggests that this inner work, though laborious, is the only bulwark against crises and temptations. It is a call to depth and authenticity.

sens: Extending far down in depth, speaking of a well or cavity
Advanced in the night or morning, speaking of the hour
Intense, marked to the highest degree
Concerning hidden, secret, or mysterious realities
G0901.detail: 1. The primary meaning is purely spatial: a deep well sinks very far into the ground, making it difficult to reach (John 4:11, the well where Jesus meets the Samaritan woman). 2. In expressions of time, the word designates the late hour of day or night: Luke 24:1 speaks of the "early dawn," meaning the moment when dawn is well established and it is almost day. 3. Applied to sleep, it expresses intensity: Eutychus sleeps "deeply" (Acts 20:9), meaning in such a deep sleep that no noise wakes him, not even Paul's speech. 4. Figuratively, the word describes what is hidden or mysterious: the "depths of Satan" (Revelation 2:24) refer to the secrets, hidden teachings that Satan wants to conceal.
G0901.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of descending and spreading out. It is formed as a simple and timeless adjective. In Hebrew, a deep well was referred to as עמק (depth, valley); the Greek βαθύς regularly translates this notion. The root expresses the image of a cavity or an extension that goes far from the surface to the depths.
G0901.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament. In three passages, it describes what sinks or extends far (the well in John 4:11, the early hour in Luke 24:1, the deep sleep in Acts 20:9). In the fourth, Revelation 2:24, it becomes metaphorical and refers to the secret or occult doctrines of the false prophets of Thyatira, ironically termed "depths"—here the word takes on a pejorative nuance, as if these secrets were dangerous abysses where error hides.
G0901.portee: This word invites the reader to discern what is apparent from what is hidden. When Paul speaks of the "depths of Satan," he warns that evil seeks to conceal itself under appearances of deep wisdom; the Christian must remain vigilant and not be seduced by dark doctrines presented as mysterious or elevated. It is a call to clarity and caution in faith.

sens: A branch cut from a palm tree, with its leaves
G0902.detail: 1. A palm branch is the foliage that is detached from the palm tree, with its long fan-shaped leaves. It is a natural element, used especially in Mediterranean regions. John 12:13 mentions it at the time when the crowd welcomes Jesus in Jerusalem: the people "took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him." It was a festive and solemn gesture.
G0902.origine: The Greek word baion comes from Egyptian: it was borrowed by the Greeks due to trade and the Egyptian presence. The palm tree being a very common tree in Egypt and the East, the Egyptians had their own name for its branches, which the Greeks adopted. It is an example of a traveling word that follows exchanges between peoples.
G0902.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 12:13. It is at the moment when Jesus enters Jerusalem a few days before his Passion: the crowd acclaims him by waving palm branches, a gesture of royal honor and festive joy. This scene recalls Jewish customs during celebration feasts, particularly the Feast of Tabernacles, where the palm played an important role. The gesture is laden with messianic significance: it is a salute to a king, an awaited liberator.
G0902.portee: For the believer, this image shows how Jesus was received by the crowd with enthusiasm: it was a moment of great hope and recognition. But it tragically contrasts with what follows just a few days later. It invites us to meditate on the true nature of Jesus' kingship: not a political kingship as the crowd may have hoped, but a divine kingship, that of the Savior and eternal King.

sens: Prophet from Mesopotamia hired by Balak to curse Israel
One who is seduced by reward and abandons the right path
Symbol of false prophets who lead believers into idolatry and immorality
G0903.detail:
1. Balaam is a prophet from antiquity, originating from Mesopotamia, known from the story in the Book of Numbers: King Balak hires him to curse the people of Israel, but God prevents him and forces him to bless Israel instead. He is a key figure in the Old Testament who appears in Numbers 22 to 24.

2. The New Testament primarily remembers Balaam for his love of reward and his unfaithfulness: although God commanded him to bless Israel, he sought a way to curse them in order to gain the reward that Balak promised him (2 Peter 2:15). This is why his name becomes a symbol of one who abandons the right path for money.

3. Balaam also represents the false prophet who, instead of obeying God, teaches the people to seduce God's people by leading them into idolatry and immorality (Revelation 2:14). The "doctrine of Balaam" refers to this strategy: rather than openly fighting Israel, one corrupts its morals from within by making them eat food sacrificed to idols and pushing them towards immorality.
G0903.origine: The name Balaam comes from the Hebrew בִּלְעָם (Bilʿam), which literally means "one who devours the people" or "one who swallows the people." It is a significant name that reflects the intention of King Balak: to hire a prophet capable of destroying Israel through a curse. The Greek has retained this name without major modification.
G0903.emploi: Balaam appears only three times in the New Testament, always in a critical perspective. In 2 Peter 2:15, he is the classic example of the false prophet who sells his spiritual services for money, thus abandoning the right path. In Jude 1:11, he is mentioned alongside Cain and Korah as a model of those who commit iniquity for personal gain. In Revelation 2:14, the Church of Pergamum is warned against the "doctrine of Balaam," which is the practice of encouraging believers to transgress Mosaic laws by eating food sacrificed to idols and committing immorality. His story illustrates how a prophet who knows God's will can circumvent it out of ambition or greed.
G0903.portee: Balaam warns us of the danger of greed in spiritual life. Even someone who has received a revelation from God can succumb to the temptation of money and power. His example also shows how false prophets operate: they do not openly fight the faith but corrupt the integrity of God's people from within. It is a call to vigilance against subtle teachings that promise to reconcile the Christian faith with the compromises of the world.

sens: King of Moab who attempted to curse Israel
G0904.detail: 1. Balak is the king of Moab mentioned in Revelation in direct connection with Balaam. He is the one who, according to the account in Numbers, hired the prophet Balaam to curse the people of Israel as they approached his lands. Although the name appears only once in the New Testament (Revelation 2:14), the reference recalls the entire story of Numbers 22-24 where Balak plays a central role: he believed that a curse pronounced by Balaam would be enough to stop Israel. Revelation names him to remind how Balaam, unable to curse Israel, advised Balak on another strategy: to seduce the Israelites through idolatry and sexual immorality. It is this ruse that worked and remains the dangerous teaching that John speaks of to the churches.
G0904.origine: The Hebrew name בָּלָק (Balak) probably means "one who devastates" or "destroyer," which suits a king attempting to destroy Israel through cursing. This name comes from the Hebrew root balaq which evokes the idea of devastation or desolation. In the Greek Old Testament, the name is faithfully transliterated into Greek as Balak, without change, since it is a foreign proper name.
G0904.emploi: Balak is the king of Moab at the time of Israel's exodus from Egypt. He appears in Numbers (chapters 22-24) as a king frightened by the arrival of the numerous people of Israel near his borders. He hires the diviner Balaam to curse Israel, but God turns the curses into blessings. Unable to curse Israel directly, Balak ultimately accepts Balaam's scheme: to introduce idolatry and debauchery among the Israelites to weaken them spiritually. This latter plan causes harm to Israel and becomes a type of the sin of religious seduction. Revelation 2:14 remembers Balak to warn the church of Pergamum against those who teach like Balaam: seducing believers to abandon moral and spiritual integrity by enticing them towards idolatry and immorality.
G0904.portee: Balak symbolizes in Revelation the danger of spiritual seduction: he represents those who seek to destroy God's people, not by force or open cursing, but through cunning that corrupts from within. For the Christian, the name Balak reminds us that the most dangerous enemies are often those who propose subtle compromises, mixing idolatry with faith or justifying immorality in the name of false freedom. It is a warning against spiritual complacency.

sens: small bag for keeping money and coins
money one possesses, financial resources
what one keeps precious, personal treasure
G0905.detail:
1. The bourse is a small leather or fabric bag that one carries to keep money and coins. It is an everyday object in the ancient world, like a pocket or wallet today. Jesus tells his disciples: "Carry neither purse, nor bag, nor sandals" (Luke 10:4), inviting them to go on a mission without any provisions.
2. By extension, the word refers to the money and financial resources themselves, what a person possesses. When Jesus asks: "Sell what you have, and give alms. Make yourselves purses which do not wear out" (Luke 12:33), he speaks of building an inexhaustible treasure in heaven by giving generously here on earth.
3. More broadly, the bourse represents what one keeps precious, what matters most to us. It can symbolize our material or spiritual attachments: where our bourse is, there is our heart (as implied by Jesus' teaching).
G0905.origine: The Greek word ballantion comes from the root meaning "to throw" or "to put inside." It literally designates the container in which money is placed. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it translates the Hebrew "kis" (purse) and "tseror" (small attached bag). It is a simple and direct word, linked to the concrete world of commerce and daily life.
G0905.emploi: The word appears four times, only in the Gospel of Luke. It occurs in Jesus' teaching on detachment from material goods. First, Jesus commands his twelve apostles to go on a mission without a purse (Luke 10:4), renouncing all human financial security. Then he invites his disciples to sell their possessions and to make for themselves heavenly purses that do not wear out (Luke 12:33), turning their gaze towards heaven. Later, after the resurrection, Jesus reminds them how he had previously sent them without a purse and they lacked nothing (Luke 22:35), before announcing to them new times when they would need to equip themselves with everything (Luke 22:36). Each occurrence deepens the tension between material detachment and concrete faith in divine providence.
G0905.portee: This word invites the believer to examine their relationship with money and possessions. Jesus does not prohibit having a purse, but he asks the disciple not to place their trust and security in it. The inexhaustible heavenly purse symbolizes spiritual investment: what we generously give in this world produces an eternal treasure. It is a word of freedom: the one who refuses to cling to their possessions discovers a divine provision that no thief or moth can reach.

sens: To throw an object, a weapon, or a projectile
To put, place something somewhere
To pour a liquid
To be thrown, to lie down
To rush, to throw oneself
To chase away, to expel
G0906G.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to throw an object, a weapon, or a projectile: "Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire" (Matthew 3:10). The image is that of a quick and decisive gesture that sends something far away from oneself.

2. The verb expands to mean to put or place something in a location: "He released the one who had been imprisoned" (Luke 23:25). Here, the movement is less violent, closer to simple positioning.

3. With liquids, to throw takes the meaning of to pour: the action remains that of projecting, but without destructive force, like pouring water.

4. In the passive voice, the verb means to be thrown, to be laid down sick: "Jesus saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth" where we find the idea of being placed somewhere.

5. In the figurative sense of rushing or throwing oneself: a wind "rushed" upon the island (Acts 27:14), the image being that of a force projecting violently.

6. Metaphorically, to throw also means to chase away or expel: the devil was "thrown down" from heaven (Revelation 12:10), that is, thrown out, forcefully removed.
G0906G.origine: The Greek word βάλλω comes from an Indo-European root that expresses the idea of projecting, throwing. In Hebrew and Aramaic, it translates mainly נפל (to fall), שׂום (to put, place), and other verbs of projected action. The family of the verb is vast in Greek: it includes many compounds (ἐμβάλλω: to throw into, ἀποβάλλω: to reject, etc.) that nuance the main action of throwing. The basic image is that of a gesture that projects something out of oneself with a certain force.
G0906G.emploi: The verb appears 64 times in the New Testament and is predominant in Matthew and Revelation. In the Gospels, it primarily denotes the concrete action of throwing: nets into the sea (Matthew 4:18), barren trees into the fire (Matthew 3:10), or even the disciples throwing the foundations of the Church. In Luke and John, it takes on more varied meanings: putting in prison (Luke 23:25), pouring water (John 13:5). With prepositions, the meaning becomes more precise: to throw "into" (εἰς) the sea, the fire, hell; to throw "on" (ἐπί) the clothes; to throw "out of" (ἔξω) the house. In Revelation, the verb becomes intensely metaphorical: Satan is thrown out of heaven (Revelation 12:9-10), the wicked thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:15). The context always reveals whether the gesture is accidental, punitive, practical, or symbolic.
G0906G.portee: This verb helps the reader understand how Jesus and his disciples act with authority and decisiveness against evil and impurity. To throw out means to reject, refuse, mark a break. Conversely, to be thrown means to be excluded, to be judged: the biblical idea of eternal judgment is often expressed by this image of rejection, of being thrown into the abyss. For the believer, the verb also invites one to reject evil from one's own life with the same firmness: to throw out vice as one throws poison out of one's house.

sens: To throw a projectile or an object with force
To place, put something somewhere
To lay down, stretch (a sick person)
To pour a liquid
To put an end to, reject
To inspire, evoke a feeling
G0906H.detail:
1. To throw something primarily means to launch it with force, especially a weapon or a projectile. This is the primary image of the word in Greek. One can also throw in the broader sense: for example, to throw a net for fishing (Matthew 4:18).
2. To place means to put something or someone in a position, a place, or a situation. This is the most common usage in the Gospels. When the widow puts her offerings into the treasury (Luke 21:1), she places them inside. When it is said that a person is put in prison (Matthew 5:25), they are placed there.
3. To lay someone down means to stretch them out on a bed, especially when they are sick or suffering. When the child is found lying on the bed (Mark 7:30), she is resting there, stretched out. This indicates that a person occupies a lying position.
4. To pour a liquid means to spill it from one container to another. When one pours new wine into wineskins (Mark 2:22), it flows out. This is a meaning close to the first, applied to fluids.
5. To put an end to or reject something means to push it away or set it aside. To say "I did not come to bring peace" (Matthew 10:34) means that the purpose is not to lay down peace, but the sword.
6. To inspire or evoke a feeling in someone means to place a movement of the soul within them. When Satan puts a thought in Judas's heart (John 13:2), he places that thought there, as one puts something somewhere.
G0906H.origine: The word βάλλω comes from an ancient Greek root that evokes the action of throwing or projecting. In Hebrew and Aramaic of the Old Testament, it translates several related verbs, notably nâphal (to fall, to throw), sîm (to put, to place), and others: the common idea is that of placing or projecting something from one point to another. The word has given rise to many compound words in Greek, each nuance the action according to direction: to throw towards, to throw out, to throw between, etc. It is a fundamental verb in common Greek, very lively and productive.
G0906H.emploi: The verb to throw appears about 35 times in the provided passages of the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and less frequently in Acts and Revelation. Its meaning nuances according to context: it primarily means "to throw" an object (a net, a knife), then "to place" or "to put" a person or thing somewhere (in prison, on a bed, in a treasury). It is also used to "lay" a sick or suffering person. In some cases, it takes on a more abstract or moral hue: to inspire a thought, to evoke a situation. The French translation varies according to the cases: "to throw," "to put," "to lay," "to bring"; therefore, one must always look at the context to grasp the exact nuance. The verb in the passive means "to be laid down, to be stretched out" (as for the sick person by the pool).
G0906H.portee: Understanding this verb helps the reader grasp how Jesus speaks of concrete and spiritual action: throwing a net to catch disciples, placing someone in prison, pouring new wine, or inspiring a thought in the heart. It is a verb of decision and intention that shows how God and men "place" acts that carry weight. Recognizing the image of "throwing" or "placing" also helps to see that nothing is neutral in the Gospel: every act has a direction, a destination, a significance.

sens: Throw an object with force, project or gesture (weapon, missile, seed)
Place, put something somewhere, especially in a direction or container
Pour a liquid
Be lying down, be afflicted with illness (passive form)
Impose or apply a burden, a penalty, a condemnation
Produce an effect, exert a moral or spiritual action (figurative sense)
G0906I.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning of this verb is to throw an object with force or intention. It is used for a weapon, a stone, or a seed that is projected: "The kingdom of God is as if a man should cast seed into the ground" (Mark 4:26). The action is direct and voluntary.
2. More broadly, the verb means to place or put something somewhere, often directed towards a specific place — in a garden, out of the house, down. When one throws a seed in their garden (Luke 13:19), they are placing it in a determined location.
3. Pouring a liquid falls into the same category: one "throws" water, wine, just as one would with a solid.
4. In the passive form ("to be thrown"), the verb refers to being laid down in bed, being ill: "Jesus saw his mother-in-law lying sick of a fever" (he was thrown into bed by the fever).
5. The verb can also mean to impose or inflict — to throw a spell, a curse, a condemnation — with the idea of causing something to fall upon someone.
6. In a figurative sense, to throw means to produce an effect or exert a moral influence: "to throw into the heart" (John 13:2) means to place a thought, a feeling in the mind.
G0906I.origine: This verb is very ancient in Greek. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of rapid movement and projection. The word corresponds in the Greek Old Testament to several distinct Hebrew verbs: notably "to throw" in the physical sense, but also "to place," "to set." Its basic image is that of a throwing gesture, of a projectile, but biblical usage extends it to any act of placing or imposing. With various prefixes (ἐπι-, ἐκ-, προ-, κατα-, etc.), it takes on nuances: throw upon, throw outside, throw in advance, throw downwards.
G0906I.emploi: This verb is frequent in the New Testament, with about 2 major usages attested here. In the Gospels, it primarily denotes the action of sowing — throwing seed into the ground (Mark 4:26, Luke 13:19) — or concrete physical acts (throwing money, clothing, the net). Elsewhere, it takes on broader meanings: pouring water, being ill in bed. In a figurative sense, it can describe a moral action, such as throwing a thought into the heart. Its complements vary: it can introduce a place ("into the ground," "in the garden"), a destination ("outside"), or remain intransitive ("to rush"). The context determines whether the emphasis is on the violence of the gesture or simply on the act of placing.
G0906I.portee: This verb reminds us that the kingdom of God begins with a simple and hidden gesture: the seed thrown into the ground. The farmer does not understand how it grows — he sleeps and rises, and behold, it grows (Mark 4:26). This teaches us trust in God: we throw the seed, that is, we proclaim the Word, but it is God who makes it grow. We are invited not to take on what belongs solely to Him.

sens: throw an object with force or speed
pour or spill a liquid
place, put something in a location
fall, rush violently
put into someone's mind or heart
G0906J.detail:
1. Throw an object with force or speed: the literal meaning of the word, that of a sudden and voluntary gesture. It is to throw a stone, to launch a weapon. By extension, it is to place something with an active movement: the serpent "throws" water like a river (Revelation 12:15).
2. Pour or spill a liquid: a nuance of the same gesture, but with fluids. Jesus "pours" water into a basin to wash his disciples' feet (John 13:5), or one "spills" perfume on the Lord's body (Matthew 26:12).
3. Place, put something in a location: the verb takes on a less violent meaning, closer to "set" or "put." The gesture remains a voluntary act, but without urgency.
4. Fall, rush violently: used in the passive or with an intransitive sense, the word describes a rapid fall. The stars of heaven "throw" their green figs — that is, they fall as a fig tree casts them (Revelation 6:13).
5. Put into someone's mind or heart: used in a figurative sense, to designate a thought or feeling that imposes itself on the soul like an object thrown. The verb then describes an invisible but also real and sudden action like physical throwing.
G0906J.origine: The verb βάλλω (ballō) comes from a very ancient root that expresses the idea of projecting with force. In ancient Hebrew, it often translates words like נפל (naphál, "to fall") or שׂום (sûm, "to put"), which shows that the image of the gesture has gradually shifted towards broader meanings: from "to throw" to "to place," from "to throw" to "to pour." Compounds with prepositions (ἀπό-βάλλω, ἐπί-βάλλω, etc.) refine this basic idea by indicating the direction or nature of the throw.
G0906J.emploi: The verb βάλλω appears about five times in the cited passages, and its meaning varies according to the context and the complements that specify it. When followed by a directional complement (εἰς, ἐπί, ἔξω, etc.), it expresses the action of throwing or casting something towards a specific place: the dragon "throws" water (Revelation 12:15). When used with liquids (water, perfume), the meaning naturally shifts towards "pour" or "spill" (John 13:5, Matthew 26:12). In the passive or middle voice, it can mean "to fall" or "to be thrown" (Revelation 6:13). The verb always retains a nuance of energy, of a decisive gesture, which distinguishes it from simple words like "to put."
G0906J.portee: Throwing is an ordinary human gesture, but it translates in the Bible invisible realities: our thoughts are "thrown" into our hearts as if by an external force; God's judgments "fall" upon the world; the sincere gift "throws" away what one possesses. Understanding this verb is to grasp that the Bible speaks of a spiritual reality with concrete words from everyday life, and that our actions — even the simplest — have a significance that transcends them.

sens: To plunge or immerse in water
To wash or purify ritually
To administer Christian baptism as a religious rite
To be overwhelmed by suffering or trial
G0907.detail:
1. In its primary and concrete sense, "baptize" means to immerse something or someone in water. It is an act of diving: one goes down into the water to be completely soaked. When Philip "baptized" the eunuch (Acts 8:38), both went down into the water; it is this physical act of immersion that is referred to.
2. The word can also refer to the ritual washings, the purifications that the Jews practiced to remain pure according to the Law. When Mark notes that the Pharisees only ate "after they had purified themselves" (Mark 7:4), he is talking about these washings of hands and vessels before the meal.
3. In the New Testament, "baptize" takes on a specific religious meaning: it is the rite by which one enters the Christian community. John the Baptist "baptized" those who came to confess their sins in the Jordan (Matthew 3:6). Jesus and his disciples "baptized" believers (John 4:1). It is a solemn act that binds one to Jesus Christ: one is "baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 19:5) or "in Jesus Christ" (Romans 6:3).
4. Figuratively, Jesus speaks of the cup he will drink and the "baptism" he will receive (Mark 10:38-39, Luke 12:50): he means that he will be overwhelmed by suffering, as if engulfed in waves. It is an image of distress and total trial.
G0907.origine: The word comes from the Greek "baptô" (to dip, to immerse), which expresses the action of immersing something in a liquid. This root has retained its primary concrete meaning: when the soldiers of Polybius cross a river with water up to their chests, this verb is used. The religious meaning of Christian baptism has been built upon this material sense: the rite consists of immersing the believer in water as a sign of purification and adherence to Jesus Christ. In Hebrew, the word "tabal" (טבל, to dip) carries the same concrete idea.
G0907.emploi: The verb appears about 70 times in the New Testament, mainly in the four Gospels and Acts. In the concrete sense of washing or purifying, it is quite rare (Mark 7:4; Luke 11:38). The religious sense of Christian baptism predominates: John the Baptist "baptizes" in the Jordan for repentance (Mark 1:4-5); Jesus is "baptized" by John (Matthew 3:13-16); after Pentecost, the apostles "baptize" believers (Acts 2:41; 8:38). The word is used with complements that specify the element or meaning of the rite: "baptize in water" (Matthew 3:11), "baptize in the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 19:5), "be baptized in Jesus Christ" (Romans 6:3). In Jesus, the figurative sense of being submerged in suffering appears: "Of what baptism am I to be baptized?" (Luke 12:50), meaning the ordeal of the Passion. What unites all the uses is the idea of transformation through immersion or solemn commitment.
G0907.portee: Baptism is not a simple rite of ritual purification, like Jewish washings. It is the act by which the believer accepts Jesus Christ and enters his Church. Understanding that "baptize" primarily means to immerse helps to grasp the weight of the symbol: plunged into the water, one dies to the old life to rise as a new creation. Baptism thus marks a definitive decision, a turning point. As for the "submersion in trial" that Jesus mentions, it reminds us that following Christ engages our entire life: we too will sometimes be overwhelmed by suffering, and it is in this that we commune with his Passion.

sens: The action or rite of immersing someone in water as a sign of religious commitment
The baptism of John, preaching repentance and preparation for the coming of Christ
Christian baptism, sign and seal of death and resurrection with Christ
Intense suffering or trial, like immersion in misfortune
G0908.detail:
1. Baptism is primarily the religious rite itself: immersing a person in water. It is a visible gesture that marks the commitment to God. Matthew 3:7 speaks of the crowds who came to the "baptism" with John at the Jordan.

2. The baptism of John had a specific meaning: it called the people to repent and prepare for the coming of the Messiah. Mark 1:4 calls it the "baptism of repentance for the remission of sins" — it was a conversion of heart, expressed by this gesture in the water.

3. The Christian baptism, which the apostles administered in the name of Jesus, means much more: Romans 6:4 explains it as a death with Christ to our old life, followed by a resurrection to a new life. It is through this baptism that one enters the Church and confesses Jesus as Lord.

4. But Jesus also uses the word in a figurative sense: in Mark 10:38, he speaks of the "baptism" he must be baptized with — he refers to his sufferings and passion, as if misfortune were a water that submerges him. It is a powerful image of trial.
G0908.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb βαπτίζω (baptizo), which means "to immerse, to dip." The basic image is that of something being plunged into water. The biblical word designates both the act (the act of baptizing) and its result (the baptism received). In Hebrew, the Old Testament does not know this rite by this name, but the Greek word has taken up this religious practice to express it clearly: it is the immersion that counts, not just a sprinkling.
G0908.emploi: The word appears 21 times in the New Testament, mainly in the four Gospels and Acts. It is always used for two things. First, the baptism of John the Baptist (Mark 1:4, Luke 3:3, Acts 13:24): it is the starting point of the story of Jesus, and it is a "baptism of repentance." Secondly, Christian baptism (Romans 6:4, Ephesians 4:5, 1 Peter 3:21): it is the sign by which the believer enters the Christian community and confesses Jesus. Jesus himself uses the word in the sense of suffering (Mark 10:38, Luke 12:50), which shows that baptism, beyond the rite, is a total immersion — in Christ, one is plunged into his love and, at the moment of the cross, Christ was plunged into suffering.
G0908.portee: Baptism reminds the believer of a central truth: your old life is dead, and you are resurrected in Christ. It is a public, visible commitment that says: "I belong to Jesus." What Jesus experienced — plunged into suffering for our salvation — makes baptism not just an isolated act, but an image of the entire Christian life: dying each day to oneself to live for the glory of God.

sens: Action of immersing or ritually washing, for purification
Jewish purification rite practiced before eating or entering the temple
The immersion or sprinkling of water as a sign of commitment to God
The mystical burial of the believer with Christ in His death and resurrection
G0909.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the physical act of immersing or washing. In Mark 7:4, the Pharisees observe the "washing" of cups and pitchers — a concrete act of ritual cleaning intended to comply with the Law.
2. It also pertains to those purification rites required by Jewish tradition. In Hebrews 9:10, these "washings" were part of the carnal regulations imposed on Israel before the coming of Christ.
3. The term can also refer to the act of immersing oneself in water as a sign of commitment to God. Hebrews 6:2 mentions "the doctrine of baptisms" as a foundational teaching, alongside faith in God and the resurrection of the dead.
4. In Colossians 2:12, baptism takes on a profound spiritual significance: the believer is "buried with Christ in baptism," an image of dying to sin and rising with Him to new life.
G0909.origine: The word comes from the verb βαπτίζω (baptizo), which means "to immerse" or "to dip." The root evokes the action of dipping something in a liquid — making it disappear under water. In Hebrew, the concept of purification by water (טבל, tabel) underlies this idea. The Greek word was taken from the Jewish context to describe purification rites, before acquiring a spiritual meaning in the New Testament.
G0909.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament. It is first used for Jewish ritual washings (Mark 7:4 and Hebrews 9:10), which served to maintain the legal purity required by tradition. In Hebrews 6:2, "the doctrine of baptisms" is listed among the foundational principles of the Christian faith, suggesting that baptism was a major initiatory rite. In Colossians 2:12, Paul gives baptism a decisive spiritual dimension: it mystically expresses the believer's union with the death and resurrection of Christ. The meaning thus evolves from external ritual to inner transformation.
G0909.portee: Baptism is much more than an act of cleansing: it is the visible sign of faith. For the Christian, it represents the commitment to follow Christ, the death to self, and the resurrection to new life. It is a promise enacted, a concrete link between the confession of the mouth and the transformation of the heart.

sens: one who administers baptism
specifically John the Baptist, the forerunner of Jesus
G0910.detail: 1. The baptizer is one who performs baptism, that is, who immerses someone in water as a sign of repentance and conversion. It is a title that designates the function or role of the one who carries out this act. 2. In the Gospels, this word primarily refers to John the Baptist, Jesus' cousin sent by God to prepare the people for His coming. Matthew calls him "the Baptizer" right at the beginning of his account (Matthew 3:1), and even after his death, he continues to be identified by this nickname (Matthew 14:2, Mark 8:28), so recognizable were his work and message of conversion.
G0910.origine: This word comes from the Greek verb "baptizō" which means "to immerse, to dip." The baptizer is therefore literally "the one who immerses." It is a functional title derived directly from the verb that describes the action of baptism. John receives this nickname because his entire ministry consisted of calling Israel to repent and receive baptism in water.
G0910.emploi: The word "baptizer" appears twelve times in the Gospels, exclusively to refer to John the Baptist. Matthew uses it in key passages about John: his introduction (Matthew 3:1), the praise Jesus gives him (Matthew 11:11-12), and the rumors after his death (Matthew 14:2, 14:8). Mark and Luke use the same title in parallel scenes. It is never a generic title for others who baptize (like the disciples), but an almost official nickname attached to the historical person of John.
G0910.portee: John the Baptist receives this nickname because his ministry defines his role with Israel: he prepares the way for the Lord. Understanding why the Gospels call him this invites the reader not to forget that John's baptism is an urgent call to conversion, a break with sin, before the coming of the Messiah. It is a reminder that baptism is never a mechanical act, but the expression of a personal decision to turn to God.

sens: To briefly immerse an object in a liquid
To dye by plunging into a coloring substance
Figuratively: to mark deeply, to impregnate
G0911.detail:
1. To dip means to quickly plunge something into a liquid and then remove it: this simple yet expressive gesture is what the rich man in the parable asks Abraham for — to dip his finger in water to cool his parched tongue (Luke 16:24). It is also what Jesus does at the table: He dips the piece of bread into the dish before giving it to Judas, an ordinary gesture that takes on tragic meaning in this context of betrayal (John 13:26).
2. To dip can also mean to dye, that is, to color by immersing a fabric in dye: thus, in Revelation 19:13, Christ's garment is described as dipped in blood — not by projection, but as soaked in blood, an image of divine judgment (Revelation 19:13).
3. Figuratively, to dip evokes the action of marking, of deeply impregnating: what is dipped into something absorbs its qualities and can no longer be separated from it.
G0911.origine: The Greek verb βάπτω comes from a root that evokes the idea of plunging or immersing. In Hebrew, the word טבל (tibel) carries the same fundamental meaning: it is the verb used to describe immersion in water or any liquid. The French word "baptism" is directly derived from it, although βάπτω itself does not denote the rite of baptism in the New Testament — rather, βαπτίζω (baptizo), a denominative verb that is closely related, is used. The family of βάπτω encompasses the concrete and simple idea of dipping or immersing.
G0911.emploi: The verb βάπτω appears three times in the New Testament according to the Segond. In Luke 16:24, it expresses the gesture of the finger dipped in water — an ordinary action of daily life for refreshing. In John 13:26, it is Jesus Himself who dips the bread, an act of communion at the table that, in John's consciousness, announces Judas' immediate betrayal. In Revelation 19:13, the verb is used in the past tense (dipped, soaked) to describe the garment of the resurrected Christ coming in judgment, soaked in the blood of judgment. The word retains this concrete and visual nuance in all cases: it is never a purely abstract action, but always a physical immersion or visible impregnation.
G0911.portee: This verb invites us to meditate on the embodied depth of the Gospel: Jesus does not ask us to understand a theology, He dips the bread and gives it. It is in these simple and material gestures — the water that moistens a finger, the dipped bread, the blood that stains the garment — that love, betrayal, and God's judgment take shape and become real for us.

sens: Jewish prisoner condemned for murder and sedition
Criminal whom the crowd chose to release instead of Jesus
G0912.detail:
1. Barabbas is a man imprisoned for a serious crime: he committed murder during a revolt against Roman authority (Mark 15:7). He is a dangerous criminal, a political agitator held with other insurgents.
2. At the time of Jesus' trial, Pilate offers the crowd the chance to release a prisoner: either Barabbas or Jesus. Contrary to what one might expect, the crowd, driven by the religious leaders, demands the release of the murderer and calls for the death of Christ (Matthew 27:20-21). Barabbas thus symbolizes the criminal that human justice prefers to save over the Innocent.
G0912.origine: The Aramaic name literally means "son of a father" (Bar-Abba). Although this name is common, it is known only through this account of Jesus' trial. Some ancient manuscripts give Barabbas the first name Jesus, which reinforces the contrast with Jesus Christ: two men bearing the same name, one a criminal and the other innocent.
G0912.emploi: Barabbas appears in all four accounts of the Passion, particularly detailed in Matthew and Mark. The prisoner is first presented as a notorious criminal (Matthew 27:16), then becomes the subject of the choice imposed by Pilate on the crowd. At each stage of the narrative, his name reminds us that Jesus' accusers chose a murderer over the Innocent. This repetition underscores the scandal of the judgment: human justice releases the guilty and condemns the innocent.
G0912.portee: The fate of Barabbas reveals the paradox of the cross: a murderer receives the grace and life that Jesus the Innocent did not receive. For the believer, this exchange becomes the very image of redemption: Jesus accepts the punishment intended for the guilty so that the guilty may be set free. Barabbas embodies each of us as sinners graced by the sacrifice of Christ.

sens: Israeli military leader during the time of the Judges
G0913.detail: 1. Barak is a military leader of Israel mentioned in the book of Judges. He fought against Sisera, the general of the Canaanite army, in response to the call of the prophetess Deborah. This man of faith is cited in Hebrews 11:32 among the great heroes of the Old Testament who triumphed by faith.
G0913.origine: The name Barak comes from the Hebrew בָּרָק (barak), which means "lightning" — an image of striking speed, quite fitting for a warrior. This name reflects his character and role as a military leader acting with promptness and vigor.
G0913.emploi: Barak primarily appears in the book of Judges (chapters 4 and 5), where he is presented as the commander of an Israelite army engaged against Canaanite oppression. Under Deborah's leadership, he charges into battle, and his victory becomes the occasion for a great song of praise. The New Testament honors him by listing him in Hebrews 11:32 among the major figures of the Old Testament who accomplished great things by faith in God, rather than by their own military strength.
G0913.portee: Barak teaches us that true strength does not come from military power, but from obedience to God and trust in His word. His name, which evokes lightning, suggests that one who acts in accordance with divine will receives superhuman strength and striking effectiveness. His example encourages the believer to respond to God's call, even in seemingly desperate situations.

sens: Father of the prophet Zechariah
Man killed between the temple and the altar according to Jesus
G0914.detail:
1. Barachie is the father of the prophet Zechariah, mentioned in the Gospel of Matthew. His name means "God blesses" in Hebrew, which expresses a divine blessing.
2. Jesus cites Zechariah, son of Barachie, as one of the innocent victims of the persecution of prophets in Israel. According to Matthew 23:35, the scribes and Pharisees killed this man "between the temple and the altar," a sacrilegious act committed in the holy place itself.
G0914.origine: The name Barachie comes from the Hebrew בֶּרֶכְיָה (Berekyah), composed of two elements: "barak" meaning "to bless" and "Yah" (abbreviation of Yahweh), the name of God. The full name thus means "God blesses" or "blessed by God." This type of theophoric name, containing the divine name, was common in ancient Israel.
G0914.emploi: Barachie appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 23:35. Jesus mentions this man in a discourse addressed to the scribes and Pharisees, listing the prophets and righteous ones that Israel has persecuted and killed. Zechariah, son of Barachie, represents the last martyr mentioned in the biblical chronology, illustrating the systematic rejection of God's messengers by the people of Israel.
G0914.portee: The martyrdom of Zechariah son of Barachie reminds believers that the rejection of God's Word and the persecution of His messengers have serious consequences. This mention encourages honoring and protecting those who proclaim the Word, rather than fighting against them. It also shows that God knows and never forgets the innocent blood shed.

sens: one who is not Greek
one who speaks a foreign or unintelligible language
one who lacks refinement or civilization
one who is considered brutal or cruel
G0915.detail:
1. The word primarily designates, in the Greek world, one who does not belong to Greek civilization: a foreigner to Hellenic culture. In Malta, Paul encounters "barbarians" (Acts 28:2, 4), meaning the local inhabitants, non-Greeks, who nevertheless show him kindness.
2. It applies to one whose language is not understood, whose sounds seem unintelligible to the Greek ear. In 1 Corinthians 14:11, Paul explains that if someone speaks a language that is not understood, he becomes a "barbarian" to the listener, meaning incomprehensible.
3. The word also carries the idea of a lack of refinement or knowledge: Paul says he is "debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to wise and to unwise" (Romans 1:14), contrasting the uneducated with the educated.
4. Over time, especially after the wars against Persia, the word took on a tone of contempt: "barbarian" evoked brutality and harshness. In Colossians 3:11, Paul mentions it alongside the word "Scythian" (a people reputed to be savage), showing that this connotation of cruelty had attached itself to the term.
G0915.origine: The word likely comes from an onomatopoeia: it imitates the sound "bar-bar" made by foreigners, whose language sounded strange to Greek ears — similar to how we say "gibberish" to refer to unintelligible speech. The Greeks used this term for all those who did not speak Greek and did not belong to their cultural world. With the political context of the Mediterranean world, the word took on a negative charge, symbolizing the foreigner perceived as less civilized.
G0915.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, primarily in Paul’s writings. In Malta (Acts 28), the "barbarians" are the island's inhabitants who welcome Paul after the shipwreck; the context shows they are kind, contrasting with the stereotype. In Romans 1:14, Paul addresses all peoples without distinction, Greeks or not. In 1 Corinthians 14:11, the term takes on a figurative sense: it refers to one with whom communication is impossible. In Colossians 3:11, Paul lists human divisions (Greek/Jew, Scythian/barbarian, slave/free) to affirm that in the church, these distinctions fade away. The meaning varies from descriptive (one who is not Greek) to figurative (one who is not understood) and ethical (one who is judged uncivilized).
G0915.portee: This word reminds us that the cultural, linguistic, and social divisions that humanity establishes do not correspond to the reality of the Kingdom. Paul uses the term "barbarian" not to despise it, but to show that God reveals Himself to all peoples and that the Gospel abolishes the hierarchies that were thought to be natural. It is an invitation not to judge by appearances or language, and to recognize in every person the image of God, even if their culture seems foreign to us.

sens: To become heavy, to be physically weighed down
To be overwhelmed, crushed by a burden or sorrow
To be dulled or slowed in one's faculties
G0916.detail:
1. The word first describes a sensation of physical weight that adds to something: the disciples' eyes become heavy and closed under the weight of sleep (Luke 9:32: "weighed down by sleep").
2. It then means to be crushed, submerged by a moral or spiritual burden: Paul and his companions in Asia were "excessively weighed down, beyond our strength" (2 Corinthians 1:8), or the apostle groans, "weighed down" in his fleshly body, longing for resurrection (2 Corinthians 5:4).
3. By extension, the heart can be weighed down, losing its liveliness and spiritual vigilance under the weight of earthly distractions: Jesus warns not to let hearts be weighed down "by the cares of eating and drinking, and by the worries of life" (Luke 21:34).
G0916.origine: The word comes from a Greek root related to the idea of weight and heaviness. It is a more recent form of a classical verb (βαρύνω). In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew כָּבֵד (kabèd), which literally means "to be heavy," and applies to the heart of Pharaoh made insensitive by God (Exodus 7:14). This family of words encompasses the entire biblical image of spiritual and physical burden.
G0916.emploi: The verb appears only six times in the New Testament, and always in the passive voice (to be weighed down rather than to weigh something down). It first describes the drowsiness of sleep: the disciples in Gethsemane have heavy eyes (Matthew 26:43), Peter sees transfigured Jesus while he was weighed down by sleep (Luke 9:32). It then expresses being overwhelmed by tribulations: Paul and his brothers in Asia experienced extreme affliction (2 Corinthians 1:8), and the apostle groans weighed down by the mortal condition of the body (2 Corinthians 5:4). Finally, it warns against spiritual laxity: hearts must not be weighed down by the pleasures and worries of the world (Luke 21:34). In all cases, the word emphasizes a form of incapacity, passivity, or loss of vigilance.
G0916.portee: This word invites the disciple to remain aware of the danger of spiritual dullness: whether it comes from carnal sleep, external tribulations, or the enchantment of the world. Jesus asks his disciples to watch with him (Matthew 26), Paul calls to faithfully endure afflictions (2 Corinthians), and Jesus warns to keep one's heart free, alert, oriented towards the return of the Lord. It is a call to vigilant sobriety.

sens: In a painful or laborious manner, requiring effort
With resistance or reluctance to what is heard
With a closed heart, insensitive to God's calls
G0917.detail:
1. The word describes an action that is done heavily, painfully, requiring effort. It's like walking in wet sand: each step demands work.
2. Applied to hearing, it means to listen with difficulty, or rather to refuse to truly listen — the ears are closed, as if numb. In Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27, Jesus and Paul describe a people who "have hardened their ears," meaning they do not want to hear the message.
3. It is less a physical incapacity than a moral hardness: the heart has closed itself through habit and resistance. The Greek verb literally means "to listen heavily," but it evokes a voluntary closing to the word of God.
G0917.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "heavy" (βαρύς, barus). Imagine something heavy, massive: it is this notion of weight that extends to the idea of difficulty or resistance. In Matthew 13:15, this expression translates a Hebrew that means "the heart has thickened" — the same idea: hardening, thickening, closing.
G0917.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the same scriptural verse cited by Jesus (Matthew 13:15) and by Paul (Acts 28:27), which itself is a quotation from the Old Testament (Isaiah 6:10). The context is one of refusal to listen: the people, despite miracles and teaching, refuse to be touched. It is a description of voluntary hardening, of this conscious resistance to grace.
G0917.portee: This word highlights a serious spiritual reality: it is possible to progressively close one's heart to the voice of God. This is not an arbitrary condemnation, but the result of repeated resistance. It should alert us to the importance of listening with an open heart, without allowing habit or doubt to harden us.

sens: One of the twelve apostles of Jesus
Disciple called to follow Jesus and share in his ministry
G0918.detail: 1. Bartholomew is one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus to be his closest companions and witnesses of his life, death, and resurrection. His name means "son of Tolmai" in Aramaic. He is listed among the apostles in the four lists of the New Testament: in Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:14, and Acts 1:13. 2. Like the other apostles, Bartholomew was called to leave his former life and follow Jesus completely, receiving direct training from the Lord and a mission to proclaim the Gospel after the Resurrection.
G0918.origine: The name Bartholomew comes from the Aramaic "bar-tolmai," literally "son of Tolmai." It is a Semitic patronymic: "bar" means "son of" and "tolmai" is a proper name. Christian tradition often identifies Bartholomew with Nathanael, mentioned in the Gospel of John, although this is not explicitly stated in the biblical text.
G0918.emploi: Bartholomew appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in the lists of the twelve apostles. Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, and Luke 6:14 place him among the twelve at their initial calling. Acts 1:13 mentions him with the other apostles after the Resurrection and Ascension, gathered in Jerusalem awaiting Pentecost. The New Testament reports no specific acts or words of Bartholomew, unlike Peter, John, or Philip.
G0918.portee: Bartholomew represents those apostles whose words or detailed acts are not preserved in the New Testament, but who received the same calling as the others and participated in the foundation of the Church. His inclusion in each of the four lists of the twelve underscores that no apostle is forgotten or less important in the eyes of Jesus, even if Scripture reveals fewer details about his life and ministry.

sens: Jewish magician and false prophet encountered at Paphos
G0919.detail: Bar-Jesus is a Jewish magician and false prophet whom Paul and Barnabas encounter during their first missionary journey in Paphos on the island of Cyprus. The name means in Aramaic "son of Jesus" (or "son of Joshua"), but this character is not religious: he practices magic and deceives people by pretending to be a prophet. He was in the service of the Roman proconsul of the island.
G0919.origine: The name Bar-Jesus is composed of the Aramaic word בַּר (bar), meaning "son of," and the name יֵשׁוּעַ (Jesus or Joshua). It is an Aramaic patronymic, common in the Jewish world of the first century. The Greek text also indicates his nickname Elymas, which means "magician" in Aramaic.
G0919.emploi: Bar-Jesus appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 13:6. Luke describes him as a Jewish magician and false prophet who opposes Paul and Barnabas during their mission in Cyprus. This man seeks to prevent the proconsul from listening to the Word of God. Struck with temporary blindness for his opposition to the Gospel, he becomes an example of the victory of the Holy Spirit over magic and religious deception.
G0919.portee: The encounter with Bar-Jesus shows that the Gospel faces opposition: false religion, magic, and deception. It also reveals that God protects His Word and judges those who oppose it. For the reader, it is an assurance that no one can thwart God's plan.

sens: Nickname of the disciple Peter, meaning "son of Jonas"
G0920.detail: This name, of Aramaic origin, designates Peter using the traditional patronymic: it literally means "son of Jonas." Jesus uses it only once in the Gospel, at the solemn moment when he changes Simon's name to Peter and proclaims him the foundation of his Church. By calling him by this family name, Jesus situates him in his genealogy and earthly identity before revealing his new spiritual vocation (Matthew 16:17).
G0920.origine: This name is composed of two Aramaic elements: "Bar" (בַּר), which means "son," and "Jonas" (יוֹנָה), the name of Peter's father. This was the common way in Aramaic to designate someone by their patronymic. The Greek transcribes this Aramaic expression as it was spoken: "Bariōnas." This nickname appears rarely in the New Testament, as the evangelists prefer to call him Simon Peter or simply Peter.
G0920.emploi: Peter, the disciple of Jesus, was originally called Simon. The name "Bar-Jonas" is his Aramaic patronymic, revealing that he was the son of a man named Jonas. Jesus uses this full name only once in Matthew 16:17, during Peter's confession of faith at Caesarea Philippi. It is a key moment: Jesus has just asked his disciples who they think he is, and Simon confesses that he is "the Messiah, the Son of the living God." Jesus then responds by calling him by his true name before renaming him Peter, marking the transition from his old identity to his new mission.
G0920.portee: This moment reveals how Jesus honors each disciple in their concrete identity before calling them to a new destiny. It reminds us that our origins and past do not define our vocation in Christ: it is his revelation that transforms.

sens: Companion of the apostle and missionary of the 1st century
Trusted man of the apostles of Jerusalem
Itinerant preacher alongside Paul
G0921G.detail: 1. Barnabas is a man from the first Christian century, a Levite from Cyprus, whose Aramaic name means "son of encouragement" (Acts 4:36). He first appears in Jerusalem as a pious and generous disciple. 2. The apostles recognize him as a trustworthy man: he helps welcome Paul when he returns to Jerusalem after his conversion (Acts 9:27), and he is entrusted with the mission of bringing the church's offerings to the elders (Acts 11:30). 3. He becomes the traveling companion and preacher with Paul: together they proclaim the word of God throughout the Mediterranean world, perform miracles and wonders, and face hostility from crowds and magistrates (Acts 13-15). 4. His role changes over time: initially presented as a support to Paul, he gradually becomes a major figure recognized by the apostles Peter and James as a pillar of the church (Galatians 2:9).
G0921G.origine: The name Barnabas comes from Aramaic: "bar" means "son" and the second element may derive from a word meaning "encouragement" or "prophecy." It is a nickname given by the apostles themselves, who recognized in this man the gift of encouragement and support. His real name is Joseph (Acts 4:36).
G0921G.emploi: Barnabas appears 28 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Acts of the Apostles and in Paul's epistles. He is first mentioned in Acts 4:36 during the presentation of his generosity towards the church in Jerusalem. Paul refers to him as his missionary companion in Acts 9:27 and 11:25. During the first missionary journey (Acts 13-14), Barnabas and Paul preach together, but Paul gradually becomes the main spokesperson. A conflict arises in Acts 15:39 regarding John Mark: Barnabas wants to take him along, Paul refuses, and the two apostles part ways. Paul later mentions him in 1 Corinthians 9:6 and Galatians 2:1, 9, 13 as a colleague and a recognized apostle.
G0921G.portee: Barnabas embodies fraternal encouragement and generosity in the service of the Church: his very nickname, "son of encouragement," reminds us that Christians are called to strengthen and comfort their brothers. His story also shows that a faithful companion of the Holy Spirit can make mistakes (the disagreement over John Mark) while remaining a valued worker. Finally, it illustrates that in God's work, some serve on the front lines while others play essential but less visible roles.

sens: Physical weight that one carries or bears
Burden, obligation imposed on someone
Difficulty, trial, affliction that weighs on the soul
Responsibility, dignity, or weight of authority
G0922.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a concrete weight that one carries: something heavy and tangible. In Matthew 20:12, the workers complain of having borne "the fatigue of the day and the heat," meaning the weight of work and effort.
2. The word also designates an imposed burden, an obligation or requirement placed on someone's shoulders. In Acts 15:28, the apostolic Church refuses to impose "any other burden" on Gentile Christians, meaning other heavy and constraining rules.
3. Figuratively, the burden becomes the affliction or moral difficulty that oppresses the soul. In 2 Corinthians 4:17, Paul calls his sufferings "our light and momentary afflictions," showing that even serious pains are light compared to the future glory.
4. In Galatians 6:2, "bear one another's burdens" means to share in the difficulties and pains of others, supporting them in their trials. It is an invitation to solidarity and compassion.
5. Sometimes, the word can evoke the weight of dignity or authority — which demands respect and seriousness. In Revelation 2:24, Jesus says he does not lay "any other burden" on his people: he exercises his authority with mercy, without overloading them.
G0922.origine: The Greek word baros comes from a root that expresses the idea of heaviness and weight. In Hebrew, the Old Testament Greek often translates this word with forms of kabod, whose primary meaning is also "heavy," "weighty," but which comes to signify "honor" or "weight of importance." The Greek word has mainly retained the sense of material and figurative weight, without fully adopting the nuance of honor from the Hebrew term. Related words in Greek include barynō (to make heavy, to burden) and barus (heavy).
G0922.emploi: The word baros appears five times in the New Testament, primarily in apostolic teaching and in the epistles. In Matthew 20:12, it refers to the fatigue of labor. In Acts 15:28 and Revelation 2:24, it designates an imposed burden or religious obligation. In 2 Corinthians 4:17, Paul uses it for spiritual afflictions. In Galatians 6:2, it relates to personal burdens and the sufferings of others. Through these uses, the word moves from the concrete (weight, fatigue) to the figurative (moral burden, religious obligation, spiritual trial), with a constant emphasis on the idea of what weighs heavily and demands effort or compassion.
G0922.portee: This word reminds Christians that life in the present world involves weights and trials — fatigue, grief, responsibility — but Scripture invites them to two responses. First, to share one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2): this is to live out the solidarity and concrete love for others. Second, to remember that even our present afflictions are light compared to eternal glory (2 Corinthians 4:17), and that Jesus does not overload us with crushing rules, but guides us with grace.

sens: Nickname of a Joseph candidate for the apostleship
Nickname of a Judas prophet in the early Church
G0923G.detail: Barsabbas is an Aramaic nickname meaning literally "son of Sabba." The term primarily refers to Joseph Barsabbas, also called Justus, who was one of the two candidates presented to replace Judas Iscariot among the twelve apostles after the resurrection of Christ (Acts 1:23). It is also the nickname of a Judas, a prophet and brother of Silas, who carried a message of peace from Jerusalem to the churches in Antioch and Syria (Acts 15:22).
G0923G.origine: The name is formed from the Aramaic "bar" (son) and "Sabba" (the exact meaning of which is unknown to us). It reflects the common practice in Israel of forming patronymic names with the word "bar" or its Hebrew equivalent "ben." It is a characteristic name of the first-century Palestinian environment.
G0923G.emploi: Barsabbas appears in the New Testament to refer to two different individuals in the early Church. Joseph Barsabbas is mentioned only once, during the casting of lots to designate the twelfth apostle (Acts 1:23): although a qualified candidate, it was Matthias who was chosen. Judas Barsabbas is mentioned with his companion Silas as the bearer of the letter from the Jerusalem council to the Gentile churches, making him an important figure in apostolic diplomacy.
G0923G.portee: These two characters illustrate that the early Church had many faithful and qualified disciples beyond the twelve apostles. Their mention shows that God chooses His workers according to His wisdom, not always according to our expectations: Joseph Barsabbas was not selected despite his candidacy, while Judas Barsabbas received a trusted mission. For the believer, it is a reminder that the Lord distributes services and positions as He sees fit.

sens: Aramaic patronymic meaning "son of Sabba"
Nickname of a Joseph in the early Church
Nickname of a Jude in the early Church
G0923H.detail:
1. Barsabas is an Aramaic name formed from two elements: "bar" (son) and "sabba" (probably a name or term meaning something notable). It is a patronymic, a nickname that identifies the person by their lineage or origin.

2. Joseph called Barsabas was a disciple proposed during the selection of Judas' successor (Acts 1:23). Although he was chosen by lot before Matthias, this nickname distinguished him among the brothers and attests to his role in the nascent Church.

3. Jude called Barsabas was a prophet sent by the Church of Jerusalem alongside Paul and Barnabas to convey the council's decision to the Christians in Antioch (Acts 15:22). His nickname clearly identified him and conferred recognized authority within the apostolic community.
G0923H.origine: The word is Aramaic, a language spoken in Palestine at the time of Jesus. "Bar" literally means "son of" and appears in other biblical names such as Bartimaeus ("son of Timaeus") or Bartholomew ("son of Talmai"). Sabba remains more opaque, but the full name Barsabas clearly designates lineage or belonging to a specific family or lineage. This type of Aramaic nickname was common in the Palestinian community of the early Christianity.
G0923H.emploi: Barsabas appears once in the Segond 1910, in Acts 15:22, referring to Jude called Barsabas, one of the esteemed prophets sent from Jerusalem to Antioch. Although the same nickname is also held by Joseph in Acts 1:23, the Segond 1910 translation renders it invisible in this latter passage (it only appears in marginal notes or certain editions). Jude Barsabas is presented as "a man considered among the brothers," indicating his prestige and authority within the Church. His sending to the converted Gentiles in Antioch shows his role as a mediator and guarantor of the conciliar agreement on the Mosaic law.
G0923H.portee: This name reminds us that the early Church was composed of Aramaic-speaking believers from the Palestinian context. Jude Barsabas embodies the trust that the apostles of Jerusalem placed in certain brothers to convey conciliar decisions: an example of communion and faithful transmission of faith between communities. His role also shows how the apostolic Church entrusted its important messages to men recognized for their character and wisdom.

sens: Blind beggar from Jericho
Man healed of his blindness by Jesus
G0924.detail: 1. Bartimaeus is a blind man who begs sitting by the roadside in Jericho (Mark 10:46). His Aramaic name means "son of Timaeus" — this is how the Gospel identifies him, showing that he is known in the community. 2. When Jesus passes by him, Bartimaeus cries out to get His attention despite the crowd's reprimands; his faith and perseverance impress Jesus, who heals him and restores his sight (Mark 10:46-52). This is a striking example of one who, aware of his need and of who can help him, is not afraid to cry out to Jesus.
G0924.origine: The name is of Aramaic origin: בַּר־טִמְאַי (bar-Timaï), where בַּר (bar) means "son" and טִמְאַי (Timaï) is a proper name. Mark reports the Aramaic name as it was pronounced in the Jewish community, which underscores the authenticity of the account and the direct link to the Aramaic spoken by Jesus.
G0924.emploi: Bartimaeus appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 10:46-52. It is one of three accounts of healing a blind man in this Gospel, and this one is particularly detailed: Mark names Bartimaeus and reports his words in Aramaic ("Rabboni"), indicating that he was a memorable figure among the early Christians. His disciples and the crowds knew his story and recounted it.
G0924.portee: The story of Bartimaeus teaches that persevering faith obtains the grace of Jesus, even in the face of social obstacles and barriers. His physical blindness and state of begging illustrate the spiritual poverty that only Jesus can fill. For the reader, Bartimaeus becomes a model: he recognizes his need, cries out to the only one who can help him, and follows Jesus once healed — a vivid image of conversion.

sens: That has weight, that is heavy to carry
That weighs on someone, that is difficult to bear
That is important, that is major
That is severe or impressive in tone
That is cruel or violent
G0926.detail: 1. The primary meaning is very concrete: a heavy burden is a weight carried on the shoulders that tires the bearer (Matthew 23:4). 2. By extension, the word describes what crushes morally or spiritually: a heavy commandment weighs on the conscience like a material burden. However, the apostle John asserts that God's commandments are not burdensome for those who love God (1 John 5:3). 3. The word also qualifies what has weight in the sense of importance: Jesus criticizes the Pharisees for neglecting what is more important in the law — justice, mercy, and faithfulness — in favor of meticulous details (Matthew 23:23). 4. A heavy letter or word is one that makes a strong impression by its grave or severe tone: it is said that Paul's letters are heavy and strong, while his personal presence would be weak (2 Corinthians 10:10). 5. Finally, heavy can qualify a brutal and cruel action or creature: Paul speaks of heavy wolves, meaning violent and merciless, who threaten the flock of believers (Acts 20:29).
G0926.origine: The word comes from an Indo-European root evoking weight and mass. In Greek, it belongs to the family of βάρος (weight, burden) and βαρέω (to weigh down, to load). In the Greek Old Testament, it mainly translates the Hebrew כָּבֵד (kabôd), which originally means "to be heavy" but in the Bible takes on the meaning of "glory," "honor," "weight" in a figurative sense. The Greek βαρύς retains this versatility: physically heavy, morally oppressive, or spiritually significant.
G0926.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and Paul. In Matthew, it describes the religious burdens imposed by the Pharisees and the major importance of certain moral requirements of the Law. In Paul, in 2 Corinthians, it characterizes the strong impression left by his letters. In Acts, Luke uses it to evoke the violent nature of the threatening wolves and the weight of the accusations against Paul. Finally, John ironically denies it: for him, keeping God's commandments is not burdensome when one loves God. Each usage nuances the word: sometimes purely physical, sometimes moral or spiritual, sometimes carried positively, sometimes negatively.
G0926.portee: This word invites the believer to discern. Jesus uses it to criticize a religion based on the weight of rules rather than on the love of God; Christian faith, paradoxically, lightens what was burdensome under the Law. John asserts that living with God is not an overwhelming burden for the one whose heart loves. At the same time, certain things (justice, mercy, faithfulness) have weight, importance — they should not be neglected. The word prompts meditation on the difference between legalistic burden and liberating love.

sens: That has a high market value, that costs a lot
That is precious, worthy of esteem and respect
G0927.detail:
1. The word first designates something that has a very high cost, an important market value. It conveys the idea of something rare and expensive. In Matthew 26:7, the alabaster jar containing the perfume is described as of great price: it is a costly object, difficult to obtain, representing a significant expenditure.
2. Beyond the material price, the expression also evokes what is esteemed, honored, worthy of value. It is a perfume that is not poured lightly: its precious nature confers a particular dignity. The act of the woman then takes on all its importance: she offers something precious to Jesus.
G0927.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "barou" which means heavy, burdensome, difficult to bear, and "timé" which means value, price, honor. The image is that of something that "weighs" in estimation, that counts a lot. This composition suggests that the value here is substantial, decisive, difficult to ignore. It is a rare word in the New Testament, used to emphasize the importance of what is described.
G0927.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Matthew 26:7, where it qualifies the perfume that the woman pours on Jesus' head while he is at table with Simon the Pharisee. This unique usage is revealing: the Evangelist chooses this term to establish that the offering is not ordinary. It is a perfume of great price, which makes the woman's act all the more significant and generous. The context highlights the contrast between the Pharisaic perception (which judges the act as unnecessary or suspicious) and the reality: it is a sincere and costly offering.
G0927.portee: This word invites the reader to grasp that authentic giving to Jesus requires sacrifice. The woman does not give an ordinary object, but something of real value, which she could have sold or kept. This shows that sincere faith is expressed through costly acts, through a generosity that does not count the cost. For the believer, it is a call to examine whether their offerings to God reflect a true esteem for Christ or remain superficial and without commitment.

sens: To torture, to interrogate by inflicting pain
To cause intense suffering of the body or mind
To afflict, to harass someone through acts or words
To experience inner turmoil due to the sight of evil
To submit to divine punishment
G0928G.detail:
1. The original meaning is to put to the question: to interrogate someone by torturing them to obtain confessions or information. It is a deliberate and methodical act of inflicting pain, as was done with the touchstone in antiquity (from which the word comes).

2. The word extends to any intense suffering, physical or moral: to torment a sick person (Matthew 8:6), which includes bodily pain and soul affliction. A demon-possessed person cries, "Do not torment me" (Mark 5:7), feeling the suffering caused by Christ's presence.

3. It also designates moral harassment: the prophets "tormented the inhabitants of the earth" (Revelation 11:10) not by physical violence, but by their words and signs that disturb, trouble, and afflict.

4. Internally, it is the moral suffering caused by the sight of evil: Lot "tormented his righteous soul daily" (2 Peter 2:8) by witnessing the criminal acts around him, which ravaged his conscience.

5. Finally, the word means to undergo divine punishment: "those who worship the beast will be tormented" (Revelation 14:10), subjected to God's judgment.
G0928G.origine: The word comes from the Greek *basanos* (βάσανος), the touchstone used to test the purity of gold and silver in antiquity. By extension, it means examination, trial. The verb *basanizô* retains this image: to put someone to the test, but through pain and suffering. That is why it applies to both judicial torture and any form of torment or punishment.
G0928G.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Revelation and the Gospels. In the three Synoptic Gospels, it describes the suffering of the sick or possessed body, and the terror of demons in the face of Jesus (Matthew 8:29, Mark 5:7, Luke 8:28). In 2 Peter 2:8, it characterizes Lot's moral suffering in the face of the corruption of Sodom. In Revelation, it regularly describes the torment of the inhabitants of the earth during the plagues (9:5, 11:10), and especially the eternal punishment of unbelievers and Satan (14:10, 20:10). The meaning remains that of intense suffering, but its object varies: sick body, soul in moral distress, divine judgment.
G0928G.portee: This word reminds the believer that suffering exists and is real: it is a courageous term in Scripture that does not minimize it. For one tempted by evil, the word shows that the righteous conscience suffers from the sight of sin (like Lot). And for the unbeliever, it bluntly proclaims that rejecting God leads to judgment and torment, which underlines the urgency of the Gospel.

sens: To subject someone to torture or severe physical torment
To agitate, shake, or maltreat (a thing or someone)
To cause someone intense moral or physical suffering
To test or examine something to verify its quality
G0928H.detail:
1. The original meaning of the Greek word refers to the torture inflicted to force someone to confess: one "tests on the touchstone" to verify the truth, just as gold is tested. In Revelation, the inhabitants of the earth are tormented by divine plagues (Revelation 12:2).
2. The word describes the action of maltreating or physically agitating: the disciples' boat is "buffeted" by the waves (Matthew 14:24), which is the clearest image — the wind and waves shake and maltreat it.
3. It also expresses intense suffering, whether physical or moral: the centurion's servant suffers "greatly" from his paralysis (Matthew 8:6), and the disciples have "great" difficulty rowing against the wind (Mark 6:48). It is the anguish that oppresses.
4. The primitive sense of testing or trial remains in the background: to be tormented is to be put to the test, tested in one’s endurance.
G0928H.origine: The word comes from the Greek βάσανος (basanos), the touchstone used to test gold and silver — the black stone on which precious metals were rubbed to check their purity. The verb primarily means "to test on the stone," then extended to the idea of torture as a means of interrogation, and finally to any form of torment or trial. This image of the touchstone reveals that to torment is primarily to test, to verify the quality or truth of something or someone.
G0928H.emploi: The verb appears mainly in the Gospels and Revelation, about a dozen times in total. In Matthew and Mark, it describes intense physical suffering (paralysis, extreme fatigue from rowing) or the agitation of natural elements (the waves). In Revelation, it takes on an eschatological significance: creatures are tormented by divine punishments. In Peter (2 Peter 2:8), it refers to the moral oppression of the righteous. The word retains the idea of trial: to be tormented is to be put to a severe test.
G0928H.portee: This word reminds Jesus' disciples, and ourselves, that trial is not absurd: it tests our faith and endurance. When Jesus walks on the waters toward his tormented disciples (Mark 6:48), he comes to those who suffer. Revelation also reminds us that the torment of the wicked is real and will one day be fully manifested — but for the elect, torment becomes a school of faith.

sens: Intense physical suffering, sharp pain inflicted intentionally
A state of prolonged distress and anguish
Punishment or penalty causing extreme suffering
G0929.detail:
1. Torment primarily refers to physical torture, the sharp suffering inflicted on someone: in Revelation 9:5, the locusts are allowed to torment men "like the torment caused by a scorpion when it stings a man," a very concrete image of acute and immediate pain.
