2. The word extends to the anguish and psychological distress that persist: in Revelation 14:11, "the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever," evoking an endless moral suffering for those who worship the beast.
3. Finally, it designates divine punishment itself, the penalty that brings suffering: in Revelation 18:7, God promises Babylon "torment" to compensate for its pride and luxury, and in verse 10 the merchants fear the "torment" of the city, meaning its destructive judgment.
G0929.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb « basanizô » which means "to torture" or "to interrogate." The root evokes the image of the touchstone (« basanos »), used to check the quality of metals: first a test, then a painful trial. In Hebrew, this concept often corresponds to words denoting pain and divine torment.
G0929.emploi: The word "torment" appears 5 times in Revelation, which is its only place of use in the New Testament. It first describes the physical suffering of men under the apocalyptic plagues (9:5). It then characterizes the eternal suffering of the wicked: those who worship the beast endure unending torment (14:11). Finally, it expresses the punishment of Babylon, the great city: it must receive torment and mourning (18:7), and this torment is so feared that the merchants dread being associated with it (18:10, 18:15). The word always carries a connotation of intensity and duration, whether it is an immediate sting or endless suffering.
G0929.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the reality of God's judgment and the eternal consequences of rejecting Christ. It is not a morbid doctrine, but a serious warning: the refusal to follow God leads to a separation from Him that is incompatible with rest and peace. Conversely, knowing Jesus as Savior protects from this torment. The word also invites compassion for those who do not yet know Christ and emphasizes the urgency of the Gospel message.

sens: One who tortures or causes someone to suffer as punishment
More broadly, one who carries out the punishments or penalties of an authority
G0930.detail:
1. The executioner is literally one who inflicts torture — bodily suffering — to punish or compel confession. This is the image of the Greek word: basanistēs comes from basanizō, to torture, and basanos, the torture rack. In Matthew 18:34, it is to executioners that the angry master delivers his indebted servant, so that the torture may compel him to pay his debt.
2. More broadly, the word designates any agent of punishment: the jailer or guard responsible for executing penalties and tortures in prisons. The executioner represents the brutal instrument of human justice, one that resorts to physical suffering to enforce obedience or extract payment.
G0930.origine: The word comes from the verb basanizō (to torture, to interrogate) and the noun basanos (rack, instrument of torture). The root evokes the violent act of subjecting someone to pain. In ancient Greek, it is a technical term of the penal and judicial administration: the executioner is a public official responsible for applying corporal penalties.
G0930.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 18:34, in the parable of the unforgiving servant. Jesus tells how a master, learning that his servant has not acted mercifully toward a fellow countryman, delivers him to the executioners to be tormented until he pays his entire debt. This context shows that the executioner is the executor of judicial vengeance, tasked with making the prisoner suffer.
G0930.portee: This parable teaches that the absence of mercy leads to endless punishments: one who refuses to forgive exposes himself to divine rigor, represented here by the executioners. For the believer, it is a call to exercise grace toward others, knowing that hardness of heart leads to a distress without escape.

sens: Touchstone used to test metals
Interrogation by torture
Intense physical or moral suffering
G0931.detail:
1. Literally, the Greek word refers to a black touchstone, used in antiquity to check the purity of precious metals by rubbing gold or silver on it. This is the primary image of the word, its original meaning.

2. By extension, this word applies to any interrogation or examination conducted through torture. It was a judicial practice in the Greek and Roman world: an accused person or witness was tortured to extract the truth.

3. In a figurative and spiritual sense, the term denotes any intense suffering, physical or moral, that torments the soul and body. In Matthew 4:24, Jesus heals those who suffer from various kinds of diseases and “pains.” In Luke 16:23, the rich man in hell is “in torment.” The word paints the agony of the condemned: a pain that tortures, crushes, and spares nothing from the one who endures it.
G0931.origine: The Greek word basanos likely comes from an Eastern language, like many technical or scholarly terms that entered Greek. Its main image is that of the touchstone: a test, a trial that exposes the truth. The Greek Old Testament uses this word to translate the Hebrew that means guilt or shame, as torture was the test meant to reveal guilt. The word has taken on all the emotional weight of inflicted suffering.
G0931.emploi: The New Testament uses this word three times. In Matthew 4:24, Jesus welcomes the sick “of pains” — the Greek text uses the plural, suggesting different kinds of physical torments. In Luke 16:23 and 16:28 (the parable of the rich man and Lazarus), the word takes on a major eschatological dimension: it describes eternal torture, the torment of the afterlife reserved for those who have rejected God. The word glides from the concrete (physical suffering) to the spiritual (damnation), revealing that the Bible never separates bodily suffering from that of the soul.
G0931.portee: This word reminds the reader that Jesus does not ignore human suffering: he welcomes and heals those who are tormented. It also shows that the rupture with God produces an endless agony. For the Christian, basanos invites us to seek deliverance from torment in Jesus and to take seriously the reality of eternal judgment.

sens: Sovereign power, royal authority, dominion of a king
Territory or people governed by a king
The kingdom of God: the messianic reign of God revealed by Jesus
The kingdom of God as a present and active reality
The kingdom of God as a future fulfillment
G0932.detail:
1. The most fundamental meaning: the power and authority of a king who governs. It is the exercise of royal sovereignty, the right to command. For example, in Revelation 17:12, some receive “royal power” for an hour — it is this power to govern that is given to them.

2. By natural extension: the territory or peoples over which this king exercises his authority. When Jesus refuses the kingdoms of the world that Satan offers him (Matthew 4:8), it concerns the inhabited lands and their peoples subjected to political power.

3. In the New Testament, “the kingdom of God” (or “of heaven”) refers to the messianic reign announced by the prophets and inaugurated by Jesus. It is the government of God established on earth and in the hearts of believers, as taught in the Lord's Prayer: “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10).

4. A remarkable aspect: this kingdom is already acting now. Jesus says “the kingdom of God is among you” (Luke 17:21), and Matthew 11:12 shows that “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence.” The disciples experience its present realities, heal the sick, and preach the Gospel.

5. But it is also a future promise: Jesus will teach his disciples to say “Your kingdom come,” showing that its complete fulfillment is awaited. Matthew 6:10 and 2 Peter 1:11 speak of an eternal inheritance, a future entrance into the permanent kingdom of Christ.
G0932.origine: The word comes from the verb “to reign” (basileuô). It originally designates the domain or exercise of royal power. In biblical Hebrew and Aramaic, it translates the words “malkoût” and “malkoûtâ,” which have exactly the same meaning: the reign, the power of the king. The expression “kingdom of heaven” is the Greek translation of the Aramaic expression that rabbis used to speak of God's reign, out of reverence for the divine name.
G0932.emploi: The word appears about 150 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (particularly Matthew) and rarely in the epistles. In the Gospels, it first refers to ordinary political kingdoms (Matthew 4:8, Mark 3:24, Luke 4:5), then broadly to the messianic kingdom of God, which is at the heart of Jesus' preaching. Jesus proclaims that this kingdom “is near” (Matthew 3:2, Mark 1:15), describes its nature in the parables of Matthew 13, teaches how to enter it (Matthew 18:3, Mark 10:15), and who inherits it (Matthew 5:3, 5:10, Luke 18:16). Paul and the other apostles present it as a present reality (Romans 14:17) and as a future entrance promised to the faithful (Colossians 1:13, 2 Peter 1:11, Revelation 11:15).
G0932.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that God reigns — not only over the universe but in the hearts of those who repent and believe. The kingdom of God is not a political or territorial matter, but a matter of the submission of the heart to Jesus. Seeking first the kingdom of God (Matthew 6:33) means choosing his will above all. Finally, the Christian lives in the tension between the “already” (the kingdom acts now) and the “not yet” (it will be fully realized at Christ's return): this hope gives meaning to all present obedience.

sens: Royal residence, sumptuous building where a king resides
In the plural, the luxurious apartments and buildings that make up the king's residence
G0933.detail:
1. The word refers to the official and prestigious residence of a king, his main building. In Luke 7:25, Jesus asks the crowd what they went out to see in the wilderness: “Those who wear splendid clothes and live in luxury are in the houses of kings” — he evokes here the luxury and comfort that characterize royal life, in contrast to the simplicity of John the Baptist.
2. The plural “the palaces” (τὰ β.) more broadly designates the entire set of apartments and buildings that comprise the royal residence — not just a single building, but the whole architectural complex where the king and his court live surrounded by riches.
G0933.origine: The word comes from the adjective βασίλειος (basileios), which means “royal” or “of the king,” itself derived from βασιλεύς (basileus), “king.” In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it mostly translates הֵיכָל (heikhal), which designates the palace or temple — the sacred or royal building par excellence. The root expresses the idea of what belongs to royal power and authority.
G0933.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 7:25. Jesus uses it to evoke the contrast between the luxury of the royal court and the austere life of John the Baptist in the wilderness. This usage emphasizes that palaces are a symbol of material comfort, wealth, and delights — everything that John voluntarily abandoned to dedicate himself to his mission as a preacher. The passage helps to understand who John truly is: not a man fond of earthly comforts, but a committed prophet.
G0933.portee: This word reminds us that the luxury and splendor of royal residences are nothing compared to the greatness of the kingdom of God. By showcasing John the Baptist who refuses the delights of palaces, Jesus invites his listeners to recognize true value: not visible and temporal riches, but God's call and justice. For the Christian, this raises a question: where do we place our true riches?

sens: Belonging to the king, concerning the king
Having the characteristics of royalty: magnificent, sovereign, worthy of a king
G0934.detail:
1. The word primarily describes what belongs to the king or pertains to his person, power, and majesty. In 1 Peter 2:9, Peter calls Christians a "royal priesthood": they form a group of priests who possess the dignity and authority of a king.
2. Figuratively, the word evokes excellence, nobility, and eminent distinction. Believers are "royal" not because they wear a crown, but because they enjoy privileges and a high status before God: they are a "chosen race," a "people for His own possession," clothed with sovereign dignity in God's plan.
G0934.origine: The word comes from the Greek root βασιλεύς (basileus, "king"). It designates what is proper to the king, what emanates from him, or what participates in his royal nature. The same root appears in the word βασιλεία (basileia, "kingdom"), which is very frequent in the Gospels when Jesus speaks of the Kingdom of God. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this term sometimes translates מַמְלָכָה (mamlacha, "royalty, kingdom").
G0934.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 2:9. Peter uses it to express the new and exceptional status of the Church: believers are no longer ordinary peoples, but a "royal" people, that is, invested with an authority and holiness that reflect God's sovereignty. This expression is set in a context where Peter enumerates the privileges of Christians (chosen race, priesthood, holy nation) to show that the Church inherits the promises once addressed to Israel.
G0934.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds them that their calling makes them nothing less than a prince in God's eyes. It is not the honors of the world that establish this royalty, but divine election and the call of Christ. Understanding that one is a "royal" people transforms the way one lives out their faith: it is to walk in a new dignity, aware of being clothed with God's authority and grace, to become a credible witness of His virtues to the world.

sens: Sovereign of a state, holder of political and military power
One who reigns over a people or territory
A person invested with royal authority by birth or conquest
Christ, presented as the messianic king of the Jews
God, recognized as the supreme king of the universe
In parables, a character representing authority and judgment
G0935.detail:
1. A king is primarily a political sovereign: the head of state who governs a kingdom and exercises supreme authority there. This is the most concrete sense: Herod is king of Judea (Luke 1:5), David was king of Israel (Matthew 1:6).

2. The word also designates any monarch who reigns, whether powerful or modest: Herod Antipas was technically only a tetrarch (a governor), but Matthew refers to him as king out of courtesy (Matthew 14:9). The Roman emperor himself is called king in the New Testament (1 Peter 2:17), as the same word applies to all sovereigns in Greek.

3. It is especially the title of Jesus: He is proclaimed "king of the Jews" at Pentecost, at His entry into Jerusalem, and crucified under this title (John 19:3, 19). This messianic title refers to the expectation of the Messiah as a descendant of David.

4. Ultimately, only God is the true king, above all: "King of kings" (1 Timothy 1:17), eternal sovereign who judges and governs the universe. In parables, the king represents God Himself, who judges His servants (Matthew 25:34, 40).
G0935.origine: The Greek word basileus comes from a root meaning "one who walks before," the initial idea being that of a leader who guides. In Hebrew, the equivalent melek has the same root. The word is universal in Greek to designate any sovereign, from small local kings to great Hellenistic monarchs, and then to the Roman emperor.
G0935.emploi: The word appears more than a hundred times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and Acts. It applies at different levels: the kings of the Old Testament (David, Saul), the contemporary kings during Jesus' ministry (Herod the Great, his sons), the Roman emperor (Augustus, Tiberius in context), Jesus Himself in His passion, and God in His sovereignty. The nuance changes according to the context: it is a title of dignity for earthly sovereigns, a messianic and ironic title for Jesus before the Sanhedrin and Pilate (where His accusers call Him "king of the Jews"), and a title of absolute glory for God. The parables of the Kingdom use the king as an image of God judging (Matthew 22:2, 25:34).
G0935.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds them that Jesus did not come to conquer a political throne, but to establish a spiritual kingdom. When He is proclaimed king, it is in faith, not by force. It is also an invitation to recognize that God alone is the sovereign king, above all human power: this frees one from the fear of the powerful of this world and directs the heart toward obedience to Him who truly reigns.

sens: To exercise royal power, to be king
To hold sovereign authority over a territory or people
To dominate, to impose one's power absolutely
To exercise with irresistible authority (for an abstract force)
G0936.detail:
1. To exercise royal power, to be king: this is the most direct sense of the verb. Archelaus "reigned" over Judea after Herod's death (Matthew 2:22), meaning he exercised political and military power as king. This is also what Jesus will do: He will "reign" forever and ever (Revelation 11:15).

2. To hold sovereign authority over a territory or people: the verb can be followed by "over" to specify on whom or what this reign is exercised. Jesus says to those who rejected His authority: "Bring here those enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them" (Luke 19:27). The reign is exercised concretely over subjects, a territory, a creation.

3. To dominate, to impose one's power absolutely: this is the aspect of domination, of supremacy. The martyrs who "reigned with Christ for a thousand years" (Revelation 20:4) exercise an authority that cannot be questioned.

4. To exercise with irresistible authority, for an abstract force: sin has "reigned through death" (Romans 5:21), and death "has reigned" (Romans 5:14). These forces act like sovereigns who control human existence without possible opposition. This is the most figurative use of the verb.
G0936.origine: The verb comes from βασιλεύς (basileus), which means "king" or "one who reigns." The Greek word is based on the idea of a person who possesses sovereign power and exercises it without sharing. In the Greek Old Testament, it regularly translates the Hebrew verb מלך (malak), which carries the same meaning: to be king, to reign over a people or territory. The root originally evokes the notion of absolute power and governance.
G0936.emploi: The verb reign appears 18 times in the New Testament. It is used in the literal sense for earthly kings: Archelaus reigned in Judea (Matthew 2:22), and Jesus Himself will reign over the kingdom (Luke 1:33, Revelation 11:15). It also applies to believers, who will reign with Christ in eternity (Revelation 20:4, 6, 22:5) or even now in a spiritual manner (1 Corinthians 4:8, Revelation 5:10). But the verb takes on an abstract and theological dimension when it describes the reign of sin (Romans 5:21, 6:12), of death (Romans 5:14, 17), or of grace (Romans 5:21): these spiritual realities "reign" as powers that control human existence. Christ must reign until the end of time (1 Corinthians 15:25).
G0936.portee: This word reminds the believer that true reign belongs to Christ alone, and that they share this reign with Him in eternal life. It also shows that sin and death are formidable powers that reign over fallen humanity — but that the grace and justice of Christ surpass and will conquer them. For the Christian, to reign means not to dominate by force, but to participate in Christ's victory and His ultimate authority.

sens: Belonging to a king, under his authority
Wearing or adorned with the insignia of royal power
Having a supreme character and governing other elements, as a king governs his kingdom
In direct service to a king, a courtier or palace officer
G0937.detail:
1. The adjective "royal" primarily describes what belongs to a king or his sphere of power — a domain, land, or jurisdiction subject to his authority. In Acts 12:20, it refers to the country of the king, the territory ruled by Herod.

2. "Royal" also characterizes clothing, the ceremonial garments that signify power: in Acts 12:21, Herod dresses in his royal robes, splendid insignia of his dignity when he sits on his throne.

3. More figuratively, the "royal law" of James 2:8 is the law that governs all others as a king governs his kingdom — a sovereign, supreme law that commands the rest of the Law.

4. Finally, "royal" applies to a person in the service of the king: the king's officer in John 4:46, 49 is a courtier, a man belonging to Herod's court who enjoys access to the sovereign.
G0937.origine: The word comes from the Greek "basileus" (king) and follows the common pattern of forming Greek adjectives: it describes anything related to a king. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "melek" (king) and its derivatives. It is a simple, direct word, without hidden connotation: it denotes belonging to the king and royal power.
G0937.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, always in a context of power or authority. In John 4:46 and 49, it qualifies a king's officer (the context suggests it is Herod Antipas), a man of the court. In Acts 12:20 and 21, it applies to royal dominion (the country of the king) and to the apparatus of royal power (the garments, the throne). In James 2:8, it takes on a figurative and theological sense: the royal law is the supreme law that summarizes all others — that of loving one's neighbor. The word thus retains its fundamental meaning of belonging to the king, but progressively rises from the literal (the garments) to the political (the territory) to the spiritual (the law of God).
G0937.portee: Understanding that the "royal law" in James 2:8 means recognizing God's governance and His Love over all the Law: this law takes precedence over the rest, it governs and judges it. This invites the Christian to prioritize the command to love one's neighbor, seeing in it the very face of the divine King. It is a powerful word on the priorities of faith.

sens: woman who governs a kingdom as sovereign
woman married to a king
woman who exercises royal power or enjoys it by her status
G0938G.detail:
1. A queen is a woman who exercises sovereign authority over a kingdom. She may do so in her own right, as a reigning monarch, or she may be the wife of a king and share in his power and honors. The word designates one who occupies the throne or is associated with the throne in all its majesty and responsibility.

2. In the Bible, the queen also symbolizes power, wealth, and independence. In Revelation 18:7, Babylon speaks in self-glorification: "I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and I shall never see mourning." She claims a security and prosperity that only a queen could feel, but this prideful speech will be followed by her judgment.
G0938G.origine: The Greek word basilissa comes from basileus, which means "king" or "one who reigns." Basilissa is its feminine form: literally "the woman who reigns." It is a simple and transparent word, built on the root of royal authority. In Attic (the dialect of Athens), it was also said as basileia or basilis. The Hebrew word from the Old Testament that this Greek translates is malka, "queen."
G0938G.emploi: The word queen appears four times in the New Testament Greek. Three of these occurrences are found in parallel accounts: Matthew 12:42 and Luke 11:31 mention the queen of the South (the queen of Sheba) who will come at the judgment. Acts 8:27 refers to Candace, queen of Ethiopia, under whose authority the eunuch whom Philip encountered served. Revelation 18:7 is the only occurrence of the word in a direct eschatological context, where Babylon speaks of herself as queen. Each time, the word designates a woman of undisputed royal rank, a figure of authority and earthly power.
G0938G.portee: The mention of queens in the Gospel reminds us that even the great of this world—kings, queens, the powerful—stand before the judgment of Christ. This relativizes human pride and trust in wealth or power. For the Christian reader, the word queen is also a call to sobriety: earthly wealth and authority are precarious positions if they are not submitted to God.

sens: woman who exercises royal power
wife of a king
female sovereign of a state
G0938H.detail: 1. A queen is a woman who governs a kingdom as sovereign. She may reign alone, as shown by the queen of the South in Matthew 12:42, who had enough power to decide on her journey to Jerusalem to hear the wisdom of Solomon. 2. A queen may also be the wife of a king, sharing his authority and responsibilities: thus, Candace, queen of Ethiopia in Acts 8:27, commanded enough to have a minister who oversaw all the treasures of the kingdom. 3. In all cases, the queen embodies female royal authority: she is not merely a figure of prestige, but a stateswoman endowed with decision-making and commanding power.
G0938H.origine: The Greek word βασίλισσα comes from βασιλεύς (king) with a feminine suffix added. It simply designates the woman who is queen, either by birth and status or by marriage. In Hebrew, the same concept is found with מַלְכָּה (malkah), which similarly means "queen" or "woman king." The image is that of supreme power in its feminine form.
G0938H.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to designate a woman exercising true royal authority. Two occurrences concern the queen of the South (Matthew 12:42 and Luke 11:31), probably the queen of Sheba from the Old Testament, presented as a historical figure capable of mobilizing resources for a long journey. The third occurrence mentions Candace, queen of Ethiopia (Acts 8:27), who effectively ruled a prosperous kingdom. In each case, the queen is not a mere royal ornament, but a woman invested with real powers of governance and command.
G0938H.portee: For the Christian reader, these examples of queens emphasize that power and wisdom are not reserved for men: the queen of the South dared to seek true wisdom in Solomon, making her worthy of the final judgment. Jesus cites this queen as an example of one who recognized the wisdom that comes from God. These accounts remind us that faith and the quest for God transcend status, gender, and position, even royal ones.

sens: Body part that allows walking
Base or support on which something rests
G0939.detail:
1. The foot is the body part located at the end of the leg, which touches the ground and allows a person to walk and stand. This is the primary and concrete meaning of the word. In Acts 3:7, when Peter heals the beggar who was lame from birth, "his feet and ankles became strong": the word here refers to the limbs that had lost their strength and that healing restores.
2. By extension, "foot" can refer to the base or support on which an object rests — for example, the foot of a statue or a column. This image, although not illustrated in the provided usages, naturally derives from the primary meaning: just as the foot supports the body, a base supports an object.
G0939.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb βαίνω ("to walk, to go"), which describes the action of moving on foot. The root thus evokes movement and support. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word regularly translates אֶדֶן ("base, pedestal"), showing that the biblical image of the foot encompasses the idea of support and foundation. The family of words around this rich root allows the Bible to express both physical movement and the idea of stability.
G0939.emploi: The word "foot" (basis) appears only once in the Greek New Testament as we have it: in Acts 3:7, during the healing of the lame beggar at the Temple Gate. Peter takes him by the hand and raises him up, and the Holy Spirit restores his strength: "his feet and ankles became strong." Here, the word is naturally used to refer to the weakened limbs that the power of God restores. It is a spectacular healing that shows that nothing resists the action of the Spirit.
G0939.portee: This healing of the beggar's feet reminds the reader that the power of Jesus Christ, continued by his disciples, is exercised concretely on suffering bodies and restores what is broken. It is an invitation to believe that Christ can transform our infirmities, visible or invisible, and make us capable of following Him.

sens: Cast a spell by the evil eye, bewitch someone
Divert someone from the truth by a bad or seductive influence
Captivate the mind in such a way as to paralyze judgment
G0940.detail:
1. The base word evokes the evil eye, this ancient belief that one could harm someone with a look filled with envy or malice. It is a form of magic or enchantment: someone looks at you and you are as if bewitched, deprived of your common sense.
2. In a spiritual context, the word rather refers to the act of diverting someone from the truth by an influence that acts like a charm or spell. The Apostle Paul reproaches the Galatians for falling under this influence: they have forgotten the Gospel he taught them, as if hypnotized (Galatians 3:1).
3. In a broader sense, it is to captivate the mind in a way that paralyzes or weakens critical judgment. The fascinated person no longer sees clearly, does not reason properly; they undergo a kind of charm that leads them away from the truth.
G0940.origine: The Greek word βασκαίνω comes from a root that evokes a malevolent gaze. In the Greek Old Testament, it sometimes translates the Hebrew verb רעע (to do harm, to afflict). The underlying notion is that of a magical or spiritual power that acts through the eyes and intention, an image found throughout the ancient Mediterranean world.
G0940.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 3:1. Paul uses it to express his astonishment and reproach at the inconsistency of the Galatians: after having heard and understood the Gospel — justification by faith in Christ, not by works of the Law — they return to legalistic observance under the influence of false teachers. Paul calls them "foolish" and asks who has "fascinated" them: the word carries a strong emotional charge here. There is no nuance between contexts: it always refers to an action that diverts from the true, that enchants the mind.
G0940.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that faith is at stake: one cannot claim to walk with Christ and be seduced by false doctrines or influences that divert from the truth of the Gospel. It is a warning against spiritual passivity — to be fascinated is to lose one's discernment. For today's believer, this invites vigilance against religious or worldly seductions that claim to offer a "better way."

sens: Take and lift with the hands
Transport by holding, carrying it on oneself
Support, endure (a moral burden, a responsibility)
Remove, take away, steal
Tolerate, endure (a behavior, a burden)
G0941.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to take and lift with the hands: the stones that one picks up to kill someone (John 10:31).
2. To carry something by holding it, transporting it from one place to another: the men who carried the coffin of the young man (Luke 7:14), or the pitcher of water that a man carries in the city (Luke 22:10). Paul himself had to be carried by the soldiers because of the crowd (Acts 21:35).
3. In a figurative sense, to bear a moral burden: to bear one another's burdens, which fulfills the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2), or to bear the responsibility for something (Romans 15:1).
4. To remove, take away: Mary thinks that someone has taken away the body of Jesus (John 20:15). Judas was taking the money that was given (John 12:6).
5. To tolerate, endure: Jesus will have to bear words that the disciples cannot bear now (John 16:12), or endure the cross (Luke 14:27).
G0941.origine: The verb comes from a root that evokes the action of holding, supporting something. In ancient Hebrew, the verb נשׂא (nasa) means "to lift, to bear," which captures the same idea of lifting and transporting. The Greek word is also used for the idea of supporting or enduring a burden.
G0941.emploi: This verb appears 27 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and the epistles of Paul. Matthew and Luke often use it to describe concrete actions: carrying a pitcher, a coffin, stones. John broadens the meaning: in addition to physical action (John 10:31), he uses "bear" to mean remove (John 12:6, 20:15) and to support a spiritual burden (John 16:12). Paul primarily uses it in a figurative sense: to bear the faith (Romans 15:1), to endure the burdens of brothers (Galatians 6:2), to bear the marks of Jesus (Galatians 6:17). Revelation uses it for patience in the face of false apostles and idolaters (Revelation 2:2-3).
G0941.portee: The word "bear" teaches us that the Christian life is not just an internal affair: it is lived in the body, in the concrete action of supporting one another. When Paul says "bear one another's burdens," he invites us to active and patient charity. It is also a reminder that following Jesus requires enduring, bearing our cross, not out of resignation but out of love.

sens: Thorny or bushy shrub, bush
Bush of brambles or thorns
The burning bush where God revealed Himself to Moses
G0942.detail:
1. A bush is a dense shrub, often wild and uncultivated. In Luke 6:44, Jesus says: "For each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thorns, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush" — this is how He refers to the small thorny shrubs that bear only wild and useless fruits, unlike the beautiful fruit trees.
2. More specifically, the bush can be a bramble, that is, a shrub covered with thorns. This is the sense in which Luke uses it when speaking of thorns that are incapable of producing good fruit.
3. The bush becomes famous and sacred in Exodus: it is the burning bush where Moses encounters God. Acts 7:30 describes it: "An angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in the flame of a burning bush." In Mark 12:26 and Luke 20:37, Jesus refers to the passage of the "bush" to remind that God called Himself "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" — proof that even when dead, these patriarchs live before God.
G0942.origine: The Greek word βάτος comes from the Hebrew סְנֶה (seneh), which designates a thorny shrub of the Near Eastern desert, probably the acacia or the bramble bush. In the Greek Old Testament, this term regularly translates the Hebrew word, notably in Exodus 3 where the famous burning bush appears. The image is that of a humble and wild plant, typical of semi-arid areas.
G0942.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, almost always in connection with two themes. The first is Jesus' teaching on fruits: in Luke 6:44, He uses thorns as an image of a bad tree that can only produce bad fruit. The second theme, much more important, is the burning bush: Acts 7:30 and 7:35 mention it in the account of Moses' calling, while Mark 12:26 and Luke 20:37 invoke it in the controversy over the resurrection, where Jesus reminds that God identified Himself there as the God of the living patriarchs. It is the symbol of divine revelation and God's indestructible covenant with His people.
G0942.portee: The burning bush embodies a profound spiritual truth: God manifests Himself not in what is great or imposing, but in the humble and despised. For us, this symbol reminds that God does not choose the powerful of the world to reveal Himself, but the humble, and that His word transforms even what seems insignificant. Jesus' invocation of the bush to prove the resurrection shows that encountering the living God is the greatest certainty: "I am the God of Abraham" — in the present, not in the past.

sens: Unit of volume for measuring liquids, particularly oil and wine, in Jewish culture
Approximately 37 liters, equivalent to just under 10 American gallons
G0943.detail:
1. The batos is a measure of capacity used by the Jews to quantify liquids — especially olive oil and wine. It is a container or a reference unit, as one might say today "a liter" or "a barrel." In Luke 16:6, the dishonest steward tells the debtor that he owes him one hundred batos of oil, which shows the practical use of the term in commercial and agricultural transactions.

2. One batos is equivalent to about 37 modern liters. This is quite a significant quantity, which makes the trade of one hundred batos of oil in the parable all the more striking: the debtor is not a small farmer, but a man with substantial business, capable of owing a large delivery of oil to the wealthy owner.
G0943.origine: The Greek word batos is borrowed directly from the Hebrew bath (בַּת), an ancient Jewish measure attested in the Old Testament. The Hebrew bath itself simply designates the container or unit, without any particular figurative origin. The Greeks adopted this term as is to refer to this foreign measure, rather than adapting it to their own units like the metron or amphora.
G0943.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 16:6. Jesus tells the parable of the dishonest steward: a debtor of the master owes one hundred batos of oil. The steward, to make friends before losing his job, reduces this debt to fifty batos. The context shows that this was a well-understood measure among Jewish listeners, familiar with large quantities of oil and wine in the Palestinian rural economy. The term here is rooted in the economic and commercial reality of the time.
G0943.portee: This parable teaches us honesty in business and faithfulness in small responsibilities. By showing the misdeeds of the steward who misappropriates his master's goods, Jesus warns us against injustice and calls us to manage faithfully what has been entrusted to us. It is an invitation to examine our own integrity in money and commerce.

sens: aquatic animal with short, powerful legs that jumps
supernatural sign or demonic creature
G0944.detail:
1. The frog is a well-known animal to the ancients, living in water and on land and characterized by its powerful leaps. In Revelation 16:13, John describes "unclean spirits, like frogs," which refers to the creature itself with its recognizable form.
2. In John's vision, the frogs symbolize evil spirits — demonic powers that come out of the mouth of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet. The image of frogs, linked in the Old Testament to the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 8), evokes here filthy creatures that bring God's judgment.
G0944.origine: The Greek word βάτραχος comes from a root imitating the croak of the frog, hence its natural and primary meaning. It corresponds in the Greek Old Testament to the Hebrew word "tzefardéa" (צְפַרְדֵּעַ), which designates the same animal. The word is used to describe the frogs of the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 8, Psalm 78:45, Psalm 105:30), which gives the apocalyptic vision a biblical depth.
G0944.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 16:13. John uses it to give a concrete and visible form to evil spiritual powers. By relating it to the Old Testament, where frogs are a plague, John shows that these unclean spirits bring divine judgment upon the powers of evil and those who support them. The image of a creeping and aquatic creature reinforces the idea of filth and the repugnant nature of these powers.
G0944.portee: This biblical image reminds the reader that evil is never presented as noble or grandiose, but as repugnant and subject to God's judgment. Seeing demonic powers compared to frogs — small and impure creatures — reassures the believer: despite their terrifying appearance, they are inferior to God and destined to be defeated. It is an invitation not to fear these spirits, but to persevere in faith.

sens: To unnecessarily repeat the same words
To talk a lot without saying much
To pile up empty words in prayer
G0945.detail:
1. The word refers to the action of mechanically repeating the same things multiple times without benefit — like someone who is senile. In Matthew 6:7, Jesus warns his disciples not to "repeat" in prayer, meaning not to believe that multiplying words will make their prayers more likely to be answered.
2. It also means to talk a lot without saying anything useful, to stack hollow words: prayer is not about drowning God in a flood of incessant words, but about addressing Him sincerely.
3. In the context of prayer, to repeat means to seek to gain God's attention through quantity rather than quality, as if God were impressed or persuaded by the noise of words — a superstition that Jesus clearly combats.
G0945.origine: The word probably imitates the sounds of awkward or interrupted speech: it comes from the Greek stammering and the concept of speaking repetitively and emptily. It is an onomatopoeic word, created to evoke the sound of superficial speech. It is related to the idea of speaking thoughtlessly, letting words flow without weighing them.
G0945.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Matthew 6:7, in the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus uses it to criticize the practice of the Pharisees and pagans who pray by piling up words, convinced that the length and repetition of their prayers will make them more effective. This word summarizes Jesus' opposition to empty formalism: true prayer is not a logorrhea, but an intimate and conscious dialogue with God.
G0945.portee: This word reminds us that prayer is not a magical technique where the number of words counts. It is a meeting of the heart with God. To repeat in prayer is to forget that God knows our needs before we express them, and that what matters is sincerity and trust, not the quantity of words. It is a lasting lesson against empty religious formalism.

sens: That which provokes disgust, horror, and absolute rejection
That which seriously violates God's law and makes it intolerable
An act or behavior morally repugnant in God's eyes
That which profanes the sacred and contaminates the holy
G0946.detail:
1. An abomination is primarily something physically repugnant, that provokes disgust: a thing or act from which one turns away in horror. The image is that of vomiting or visceral rejection.

2. In the Bible, the word designates what deeply violates God's law and holiness, making it intolerable in His eyes. This is why Jesus says in Luke 16:15 that what is "exalted among men" — pride, the pretense of righteousness — "is an abomination before God": what men glorify, God finds repugnant.

3. An abomination can be a particular act, such as idolatry or lying (Revelation 21:27: "Nothing impure will enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false").

4. It can also be a prophetic reality: "the abomination of desolation" (Matthew 24:15, Mark 13:14) is a profanation of the temple that announces destruction. In Revelation 17:4-5, the abominations refer to all the impure and idolatrous acts of great Babylon.
G0946.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that expresses violent and physical rejection, like vomiting. In Hebrew, the Bible uses two main words: תּוֹעֵבָה (tôʿéba, "moral abomination") and שֶׁקֶץ (sheqets, "unclean thing"). The Greek word captures this dual notion: a moral disgust and a religious impurity. It is a visceral feeling that God Himself experiences in the face of what violates His holiness.
G0946.emploi: The word "abomination" appears 6 times in the Segond, almost always in an eschatological or moral sense. In the Synoptics (Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14), it refers to the abomination of desolation, a profanation of the temple foretold by Daniel and a sign of the end. In Luke (16:15), Jesus applies it to human pride and the false righteousness of the Pharisees. In Revelation, John uses it to describe moral and idolatrous impurities: the abominations fill the cup of Babylon (17:4-5) and exclude from eternal heaven (21:27). Each time, the abomination marks an absolute rupture with God's will and holiness.
G0946.portee: This word reminds Christians of God's radical holiness and His absolute intolerance of sin. It is not merely disapproval, but visceral rejection. It warns us that what the world honors — wealth, prestige, the appearance of virtue — can be an abomination in God's eyes. Finally, it assures us that in eternal heaven, nothing impure will have access to God's presence: it is a call to purity of heart and sanctification.

sens: That which provokes disgust, horror, that is rejected with repugnance
That which is contrary to God's will and nature, morally detestable
G0947.detail:
1. The word describes something intrinsically repugnant, that inspires disgust and rejection. It is the image of one who provokes visceral aversion: one cannot bear it. In Titus 1:16, Paul describes the works of those who claim to know God but deny Him by their conduct as abominable — their acts are so repugnant that they revolt.
2. On a moral and religious level, abominable means what offends God, what violates His holiness and commandments. It is a judgment of absolute value: these works are not merely bad, they are detestable in the eyes of the Most High, provoking His rejection.
G0947.origine: The word comes from the verb βδελύσσω (bdélysso), which means to abhor, to reject with disgust. This Greek family evokes a physical reaction of aversion. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word often translates the Hebrew תּוֹעֵבָה (toéva), which designates what is abominable in the Lord's eyes — notably idolatrous practices or behaviors that transgress His law.
G0947.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:16. Paul addresses the Cretans to describe false Christians who claim to know God with their mouths but deny Him by their evil works. These works are described as abominable: they are not ordinary failings, but acts that revolt, that radically contradict the profession of faith. The context emphasizes that true knowledge of God is measured by the coherence between word and action.
G0947.portee: This word reminds us that God is not indifferent to our actions: He judges works, not just displayed intentions. For the reader, it poses a demanding question: do my actions correspond to my profession of faith? A life in glaring contradiction to the Gospel is not merely imperfect — it is abominable, it dishonors the name of God that one claims to serve.

sens: To feel a visceral repugnance, a deep disgust towards something or someone
To consider as detestable, repulsive, unworthy
To reject with horror what offends God or the conscience
G0948.detail:
1. The word first evokes a physical reaction: to have something in abomination means to be disgusted by it to the point of turning away, as one would turn away from something that stinks. In Romans 2:22, the one who "has in abomination the idols" considers them with instinctive horror, as if they literally reeked.

2. The meaning then broadens: it is to judge something as profoundly evil, morally repugnant. Abomination pertains to acts, creatures, or states that offend God or justice.

3. In Revelation 21:8, the "abominable" are those who have committed acts so repugnant (murder, impurity, lying) that they deserve eternal rejection. The word then designates the character of what cannot exist in the presence of God.
G0948.origine: The Greek verb comes from a root expressing foulness (βδέω, to smell bad): the starting image is that of sensory disgust. In translating the Greek Old Testament, this word primarily renders the Hebrew תּעב (ta'ab), which also means "to have in horror, to consider as an abomination." It is a vocabulary of absolute rejection, blending the physical (the repugnant) and the spiritual (the offense to God).
G0948.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Greek New Testament. In Romans 2:22, Paul places it at the heart of an accusation: the Jew who "has in abomination the idols" commits sacrilege, adultery — he is therefore hypocritical, as he rejects the practices of idolaters while imitating their sins. In Revelation 21:8, the adjective "abominable" qualifies the sinners excluded from the Kingdom: murderers, liars, the impure. The word always carries an absolute, irrevocable moral condemnation.
G0948.portee: This word invites the reader to become aware of the gravity of sin in the eyes of God. It is not a matter of simple disagreement or flaw: abomination is what is radically repugnant, what cannot coexist with the holiness of God. At the same time, Romans 2:22 warns: it is easy to "hate" evil in others while committing it oneself. It is a call to moral honesty and repentance.

sens: Firmly established, stable, not shaken
Having legal force, valid and enforceable
Certain, trustworthy, guaranteed
G0949.detail:
1. An object or construction that is firmly established: an anchor is "sure" (Hebrews 6:19) because it holds firm and penetrates deeply, not yielding to storms.
2. An act or decision that has legal effect and binding force: a will is only fully valid "in case" of the testator's death (Hebrews 9:17), otherwise it does not bind anyone.
3. A spiritual reality or a promise from God that is certain and unshakeable: God's promise is "assured" to all heirs because it rests on grace, not on the law (Romans 4:16); the hope we possess is "sure" in times of trouble (2 Peter 1:19).
G0949.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to walk," "to go." A thing that is bébaios is something one can walk on without fear of it giving way: it is solid underfoot. The image is that of firm ground, a foundation that does not collapse. In Greek, the word opposes what is unstable, doubtful, or revocable.
G0949.emploi: The word appears about 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in the letters of Paul and Peter. Paul uses it to speak of God's promise to Abraham, which remains certain despite the law (Romans 4:16). The letter to the Hebrews uses it to describe the anchor of the soul, the irrevocable effect of the word, and the validity of the will (Hebrews 6:19; 2:2; 9:17). Peter uses it to affirm that we must "make sure" of our calling and election (2 Peter 1:10), and that the prophetic word is particularly certain (2 Peter 1:19). In each context, the word emphasizes that what is bébaios cannot be questioned or annulled.
G0949.portee: For the believer, this word speaks of the unshakeable nature of what God promises and accomplishes. The promise is not fragile or subject to revision: it remains "assured" even when faith is tested. It is an invitation to rest our hearts and trust on the stable foundations that God alone offers, and to correspond to this certainty by affirming our own calling.

sens: To make firm, solid, stable
To confirm the truth or validity of something
To establish someone in perseverance or faith
To guarantee, ensure the realization of what has been promised
G0950.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to make something physically or morally firm and stable, like consolidating a foundation. It is the image of a structure becoming solid and unshakeable: "being rooted and built up in him, and established in the faith" (Colossians 2:7).

2. The word also means to confirm the truth, validity, or authenticity of something — to affirm that it is true and reliable. When the Lord "confirmed the word by the signs" (Mark 16:20), he attested by facts that this word was true.

3. Applied to people, it means to establish someone durably in a position, conviction, or faithfulness. "He will also establish you to the end" (1 Corinthians 1:8) means that God will support the unshakeable believers until the judgment.

4. The word also carries the idea of guaranteeing the realization of a promise or commitment: "confirming the promises made to the fathers" (Romans 15:8) means that Christ has made these promises certain and fulfilled.
G0950.origine: The word comes from the adjective βέβαιος (bebaia, "firm, stable, assured"), which rests on the root of βαίνω (bainō, "to go, to stand"). The same family is found in other words that express stability and solidity. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this verb often translates words meaning "to establish" or "to set up" (like קוּם, qoum, "to rise, to stand"), which share the image of what does not waver.
G0950.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's letters. It is used to confirm a word or promise (Mark 16:20: God "confirmed" the word; Romans 15:8: Christ "confirming" the promises). It also applies to God's action on believers: to establish someone in faith or until the final judgment (1 Corinthians 1:8; 2 Corinthians 1:21). In the passive form, it describes the state of one who is firmly established: testimonies and teachings are "solidly established" among the readers (1 Corinthians 1:6; Colossians 2:7). In each context, the word emphasizes not just a simple statement, but a stable and guaranteed reality.
G0950.portee: This word reminds the believer that God not only speaks but acts to make his promises certain and stable. It assures that faith is not fragile or floating, but that God supports and establishes it until the end. It is a word of encouragement for those who fear to waver or weaken: God himself works to keep us standing in faith.

sens: The action of making firm, confirming something that was doubtful or contested
A proof, an attestation that establishes the truth of a statement
A solid guarantee, an oath that ends disputes
G0951.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of making something firm and certain. When Paul speaks of "the confirmation of the Gospel" (Philippians 1:7), he means the defense and solidification of the Christian faith: it is to establish, consolidate, show that the Gospel is true and enduring.
2. It can also mean an attestation, a proof that confirms what was in question. This is the sense of an official validation.
3. In a legal or commercial context, it is a guarantee or an oath that makes an agreement definitive. In Hebrews 6:16, the human oath functions as a "guarantee" that resolves any dispute: the promise made under oath can no longer be contested.
G0951.origine: The word comes from the adjective "bebaíos" (firm, stable, certain), which is itself formed from the root "baínō" (to go, to walk). The original image is that of something established solidly, on a stable foundation. The form "bebaiōsis" thus designates the process or result of this stabilization. It is a word from the family of the verb "bebaiōō" (to confirm, to make firm).
G0951.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament according to the provided usages. In Philippians 1:7, Paul uses it to refer to the entire work of defending and confirming the Gospel among believers and the world. In Hebrews 6:16, it takes on a more legal and commercial sense: the oath serves as a "guarantee" that resolves disputes and makes an agreement indisputable. In this latter context, the word reflects a common practice: the oath was a legal mechanism to provide unshakeable certainty.
G0951.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that our faith is not based on doubt or uncertainty, but on the confirmation and guarantee that God gives us. It also emphasizes that the Gospel must be defended and strengthened, not just passively believed. And it shows that God, by taking an oath, gives us the strongest guarantee of His promises.

sens: That which can be trampled underfoot, accessible to all
That which is not consecrated to God, contrary to the sacred
Lacking respect for holy things
Empty, without moral or spiritual value
Referring to a person who is irreligious or impious
G0952.detail:
1. The word first evokes the image of a threshold that one treads without fear: profane means that which is accessible, that which can be crossed without reverence, in contrast to the sanctuary closed to the uninitiated.

2. In a religious sense, profane designates everything that does not belong to the sacred domain, that which is not consecrated to God — a strong contrast that Paul establishes in 1 Timothy 4:7 when he commands to reject "profane and absurd myths."

3. The word carries a value judgment: to call something "profane" means that it lacks respect for God and holy realities — that is why Timothy must "avoid vain and profane talk" (2 Timothy 2:16), which leads away from true piety.

4. Profane also qualifies that which is hollow, devoid of true meaning, mere chatter without spiritual foundation — such vain discourse opposes sound doctrine.

5. Applied to a person, the word describes one who despises holy things or lives without regard for God: Esau is called "profane" (Hebrews 12:16) because he sold his birthright for a meal, thereby showing that he attached no value to spiritual realities.
G0952.origine: The Greek word comes from the idea of "crossing the threshold" (root βαίνω, "to walk"). In Hebrew from the Old Testament, we encounter similar words that designate what is ordinary, common, not consecrated (notably חֹל). The natural contrast is made with ἱερός (sacred, holy), for what is profane is precisely what is outside the realm of divine holiness — that which can be trampled, treated without particular regard.
G0952.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Pauline epistles and in the epistle to the Hebrews. Paul primarily uses it to describe discourse or myths (1 Timothy 4:7; 6:20; 2 Timothy 2:16) that must be avoided because they divert from true faith and produce impiety. It also designates categories of people: in 1 Timothy 1:9, the "profane" (the impious without respect for God) are listed alongside murderers and parricides. In Hebrews 12:16, Esau embodies the very type of the profane, one who despises what is sacred. The meaning thus oscillates between profane things (vain words) and profane people (lived or characterized by a disdain for holy realities).
G0952.portee: This word invites the believer to discern what belongs to the sacred and what does not, and to cultivate respect for the things of God. For Timothy and for us, it is about being vigilant against empty words that claim wisdom but lead away from true piety. The contrast between profane and sacred reminds us that our language, thoughts, and choices must bear the mark of reverence toward God, not spiritual indifference.

sens: To violate the sacred character of something consecrated to God
To treat with disrespect what is holy
G0953.detail:
1. To profane is to violate the sacred character of something consecrated to God. The word evokes the image of soiling or diverting respect from what should remain untouched and pure. Jesus tells the Pharisees that the priests "profane the Sabbath" by performing their service in the temple on the day of rest (Matthew 12:5): they transgress the law of rest, but legally, to honor God. 
2. To profane is also to treat with disrespect or contempt what is holy. It is to willfully outrage what belongs to God. Paul's accusers suspect him of having attempted to "profanate the temple" (Acts 24:6), in other words, to soil or desecrate it through an impious act.
G0953.origine: The word comes from the Greek bébelos, which literally means "that which can be trampled underfoot," "that which is not forbidden to access." It stands in opposition to what is sacred, to what cannot be touched without sin. By adding the verb "to make," we get "to render profane," "to remove the sacred character." This verb often translates the Hebrew verb "ḥalal" (חלל), which carries the idea of digging, piercing, violating, profaning.
G0953.emploi: The verb to profane appears only twice in the New Testament. Matthew 12:5 uses it to describe how the priests, by their ministry in the temple on the Sabbath, technically seem to transgress the rest: Jesus uses it to justify His own act of healing on the Sabbath. Acts 24:6 uses it in the accusations against Paul: his opponents fear that he wanted to soil the temple, to attack its holiness. In both cases, the word touches the heart of the relationship to God: the respect or contempt of what is consecrated to Him.
G0953.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that certain things belong to God and deserve our respect. It invites us to discern between the external transgression of the Law and the true intention: Jesus shows that the Sabbath can be "profaned" technically by doing good, for the Law serves life and the love of God. The word also warns: to profane the holy is to contest the lordship of God.

sens: Prince of demons, chief of the evil spiritual world
Satan or an alternative name for the adversary of God
Accusation made against Jesus to explain his healing miracles
G0954.detail:
1. Beelzebul is presented in the New Testament as the prince of demons, that is, the chief of evil spirits. In Mark 3:22, the scribes say that Jesus "is possessed by Beelzebul; it is by the prince of demons that he casts out demons." The name designates the highest authority of the spiritual world hostile to God.
2. Beelzebul is a name given to Satan himself, the main enemy of God and humanity. Jesus claims that the accusations of the Pharisees divide the camp of evil: in Luke 11:18, he asks, "If Satan is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand?" The use of the name "Beelzebul" and "Satan" as equivalents shows that they refer to the same hostile reality.
3. The Pharisees accuse Jesus of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebul. This is an attempt to discredit his miracles by claiming that they come from evil rather than from God. Jesus responds to this accusation in Matthew 12:27: "If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out?"
G0954.origine: The name comes from Hebrew, combining "Baal" (lord) with a second term referring either to flies or to a dwelling or refuse. It is a transformation of the ancient title "Baal Zebub" (lord of the flies), a name of a deity worshiped in Canaanite paganism that the prophets of Israel mocked. In the time of Jesus, the word designates Satan or his chief lieutenant in the kingdom of darkness.
G0954.emploi: Beelzebul appears only in the Gospels, in seven verses spread across Matthew, Mark, and Luke. It always refers to the same incident: religious leaders or people in the crowd accuse Jesus of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebul. Jesus responds to this accusation by demonstrating its illogicality: how would Satan cast out his own servants? This accusation shows the hostility of the religious authorities towards the signs of the Messiah and their spiritual blindness. The name reveals how Jesus' enemies attempted to supernaturally explain what they could not deny naturally.
G0954.portee: For the believer, this passage teaches that Jesus has won a victory over the world of evil and that no divided kingdom can stand. It also shows the danger of a hardened heart that sees the works of God and attributes them to the devil out of malice or blindness. It is a warning against blaspheming the Holy Spirit, which consists of deliberately rejecting the evidence of divine power.

sens: A name to designate Satan, the enemy of God and His children
G0955.detail: 1. Belial is a title or nickname that Satan bears in biblical vocabulary, particularly in the New Testament. It designates the spiritual adversary, the prince of darkness opposed to Christ. In 2 Corinthians 6:15, Paul uses this name to show the radical opposition between Christ and Satan: "What accord has Christ with Belial?" — the rhetorical question emphasizes that there is none, just as between light and darkness.
G0955.origine: Belial comes from Hebrew and literally means "worthlessness" or "uselessness" (from two roots: "without" and "profit"). This name circulated in intertestamental Judaism to designate personified evil and Satan himself. The word already appears in the Hebrew Old Testament, notably in 1 Samuel 1:16, to qualify a morally worthless woman; it comes to be applied to the Enemy as the very embodiment of the absence of good and opposition to God. The two forms — Βελίαλ and Βελιάρ — circulated in ancient Greek manuscripts, the latter perhaps reflecting a regional pronunciation.
G0955.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in 2 Corinthians 6:15. Paul uses it to warn Christians against the idea of associating with unbelievers. He poses a series of rhetorical questions intended to show the impossibility of an alliance between two opposing worlds — the kingdom of Christ and that of Belial. This unique occurrence shows that this name was familiar to Greek-speaking Christian readers as a traditional designation of Satan.
G0955.portee: This name reminds the Christian that Satan is not an abstract or neutral force, but the personal Enemy of God, characterized by his spiritual uselessness and total opposition to good. The invocation of Belial by Paul exhorts us not to seek compromise with the world of sin, but to recognize that following Christ requires a clear separation from what opposes Him.

sens: projectile shot from a bow
arrow or similar object intended to wound
malicious attack or hurtful word
G0956.detail:
1. The dart is primarily a projectile of war shot from a bow — an arrow or a similar object designed to fly through the air and strike its target.
2. By extension, the word more broadly designates any sharp object intended to wound or destroy: a spear, an arrow.
3. In a figurative sense, the dart represents a sudden and hurtful attack — a word that hurts, an accusation, a temptation of evil. It is in this sense that Paul speaks of the "fiery darts of the wicked" (Ephesians 6:16): the temptations and spiritual attacks that Satan launches against the believer, which can be parried with the shield of faith.
G0956.origine: The word comes from the verb "ballô" (to throw, to cast), which is also the root of the concept of projection and violent movement. In ancient Hebrew, the same concept is rendered by "chetz," which designates both the material arrow and the spiritual attack. The family of this word includes all terms related to the action of projecting or striking from a distance.
G0956.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 6:16. Paul uses it in his description of the spiritual armor of the believer: he lists the protections (belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, shoes of peace, shield of faith, helmet of salvation, sword of the Spirit), and the fiery dart specifically represents the attacks of the wicked against which the believer must defend himself. The context of the passage — an exhortation to spiritual warfare — transforms the warrior dart into a metaphor for the temptation and doubt that Satan sends.
G0956.portee: This passage invites the believer to recognize that the Christian life is a real spiritual battle, and that we are targets. The fiery darts of the wicked are not gross lies, but subtle temptations — doubt, guilt, fear, despair — that aim to divert us from faith in Jesus Christ. Paul assures us that the shield of faith can extinguish them: that is, trust in God and His love for us, based on the truth of the Gospel, is our best protection against these attacks.

sens: In a more appropriate, suitable, or advantageous manner
More completely or assuredly
More correctly, with greater accuracy
G0957.detail:
1. The word denotes what is better, more suitable, or more advantageous — the idea of superiority in quality or appropriateness. In 2 Timothy 1:18, Paul tells Timothy: "You know better than anyone" — meaning more fully, more directly than anyone else — what services Onesiphorus rendered in Ephesus.
2. The adverb "better" can also express greater certainty or assurance: "you know better" means that Timothy is in a position to know more surely and completely than others.
3. Generally, the word refers to what is superior or preferable when comparing possibilities or ways of doing things — a more just or appropriate manner.
G0957.origine: This word is a comparative form of the adjective "good" (ἀγαθός in Greek). It expresses the idea that something surpasses in quality what is ordinary or what surrounds it. The family of the word includes all terms related to goodness and excellence. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew "tov" (good), showing that Greek follows the same logic of appreciation and evaluation.
G0957.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament (2 Timothy 1:18), used as an adverb. Paul appeals to Timothy's privileged knowledge: he has a more direct and complete understanding than Paul himself of the benevolent actions of Onesiphorus in Ephesus. The context shows that "better" emphasizes not an abstract comparison, but a concrete superiority of knowledge or position to judge a situation.
G0957.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that certain people, through their closeness or experience, know better than others the true works of goodness accomplished in secret. It invites us to recognize and honor those who serve faithfully, even when few people see it — and to question what we truly know about the service of others.

sens: Youngest son of Jacob and Rachel, eponymous ancestor of a tribe of Israel
The tribe descended from Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes of Israel
A member of this tribe
G0958.detail:
1. Benjamin is the youngest son of Jacob and his wife Rachel (Genesis 35:18). His name means "son of the right hand" in Hebrew, symbolizing favor and blessing. He is the founding ancestor of a tribe that bears his name.

2. The tribe of Benjamin is one of the twelve tribes of Israel. It occupied a small territory between Judah and Ephraim, in the center of the land. Revelation 7:8 counts it among the sealed and saved tribes at the end of times.

3. Every Israelite descended from this tribe is called a Benjamite. The Apostle Paul identifies himself as "of the tribe of Benjamin" (Romans 11:1 and Philippians 3:5), showing his identity and rootedness in the chosen people. King Saul, whom God gave to Israel, was also from this tribe (Acts 13:21).
G0958.origine: The Hebrew name בֶּנְיָמִין (Binyamin) literally means "son of the right hand" (ben = son, yamin = right hand). In the ancient East, the right side was a symbol of strength, honor, and blessing. This is why this name expresses divine favor. Benjamin received this name at his birth because his mother Rachel, dying in childbirth, first called him "Ben-Oni" (son of my sorrow), but Jacob renamed him "Benjamin" to express his hope.
G0958.emploi: Benjamin appears four times in the New Testament, always as a proper name. It refers either to the historical figure (the founding ancestor) or to the tribe that descends from him. Paul cites his own belonging to the tribe of Benjamin to affirm his identity as an authentic Israelite (Romans 11:1 and Philippians 3:5) — it was a point of genealogical honor. King Saul is identified as "of the tribe of Benjamin" (Acts 13:21), reminding us that it was from this tribe that the first king of Israel came. Finally, in the vision of the Book of Revelation, Benjamin is among the twelve tribes, each receiving God's seal (Revelation 7:8), a symbol of protection and salvation.
G0958.portee: The name Benjamin reminds the Christian reader that God chooses the weak and the small: a small tribe, a young beloved son of his father. Paul claims this identity to show that even a "pure-blooded" Israelite can recognize Jesus and enter into God's plan of salvation. Benjamin's presence in the divine seal in Revelation affirms that all tribes and all heirs of God's people will be gathered and saved.

sens: Daughter of King Herod Agrippa I
Woman of the royal court in the first century
Witness of the trial of the Apostle Paul in Caesarea
G0959.detail: Berenice is the daughter of King Herod Agrippa I, a descendant of the Herodian family that ruled in Judea during the New Testament period. She appears in the account of Paul's trial in Caesarea, where she accompanies her brother King Agrippa: "King Agrippa and Berenice arrived at Caesarea to greet Festus" (Acts 25:13). She attends the public hearing of Paul, in the official venue of the hearing (Acts 25:23), in great pomp alongside Roman and Jewish authorities. At the end of Paul's defense speech, she rises with her brother and all the attendees (Acts 26:30), a silent but present figure of the political and religious context in which the apostle testifies to his faith.
G0959.origine: Berenice is a Greek name of Macedonian origin, a variant of Pherenike, literally meaning "she who brings victory" (from the Greek phérein, "to bring," and nikē, "victory"). This name was common in Hellenistic royalty. Berenice herself bears this royal name typical of the dynasties that followed Alexander the Great.
G0959.emploi: Berenice appears only three times in the New Testament, exclusively in the three chapters of the Book of Acts dedicated to Paul's trial before the Roman governor Festus and King Agrippa (Acts 25-26). She is never described by her words or her own actions, but only as the companion of her brother Agrippa, her elder brother. Her role is purely contextual: she represents the framework of royal and Judeo-Roman power in which Paul appears and testifies. Her silence even underscores that the center of the passage is not the court, but the defense of the Gospel.

sens: City in Macedonia located in northern Greece, a main stop on Paul's second mission
G0960.detail: 1. Berea is an ancient city in Macedonia, in northern Greece. It appears in the account of Paul's second apostolic mission: fleeing the persecution of the Jews in Thessalonica, Paul and Silas take refuge there at night (Acts 17:10), find a welcoming synagogue, and preach the Gospel. The Jews from Thessalonica, irritated by the success of Paul's message, pursue him to Berea to stir up trouble (Acts 17:13).
G0960.origine: The name Berea (in Greek Βέροια, Beroia) designates a historically significant city in northern Greece. Its etymology is unclear. It is one of the main cities in the region of Macedonia, often mentioned by ancient historians as a commercial and administrative center, and it became famous in the history of early Christianity thanks to the Apostle Paul.
G0960.emploi: Berea appears twice in Acts, exclusively in the context of Paul's second mission in Greece (around 50 AD). After being chased out of Thessalonica by a crowd stirred up by hostile Jews, Paul and Silas go to Berea, where the reception is more favorable: the inhabitants examine the Scriptures diligently to verify Paul's words (Acts 17:11, although not cited here in detail). However, the adversaries from Thessalonica pursue them and disturb this community as well. Berea represents in Acts a place of temporary refuge and preaching, but also of persistent confrontation with religious hostility.
G0960.portee: Berea reminds us that the preaching of the Gospel encounters obstacles, even in cities where the context seems more welcoming. It also illustrates Paul's tenacity in his mission despite persecutions. For the Christian reader, Berea embodies the possibility of a receptive and verified faith in the Scriptures, but also the reality that opposition to the Christian message can cross boundaries and that borders do not stop those who seek to stifle the word of God.

sens: inhabitant of the city of Berea, in Macedonia
G0961.detail: 1. The word designates someone who comes from Berea, an important city in Macedonia (northern Greece). It is an adjective that indicates the geographical origin of a person, similar to saying "Parisian" or "Marseillais." In Acts 20:4, Sopater is described as "of Berea," which shows that he was from this city and accompanied the apostle Paul on his missionary journeys.
G0961.origine: The word comes from the Greek name of the city of Berea (Βέροια in Greek). It is an adjective formed from the name of the place, according to the usual practice in ancient languages: adding a suffix (here -αῖος) to the name of a city or region to mean "belonging to, coming from." This same adjective is found for other Macedonian cities mentioned in Acts.
G0961.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:4. There it designates Sopater, a traveling companion of the apostle Paul. This passage lists the assistants and delegates who accompanied Paul on his return to Jerusalem after his third missionary journey. Sopater represents the churches of Macedonia among this group of faithful disciples who support the apostle in his ministry.

sens: Village located near Jerusalem, about three kilometers east of the city
Place where Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead
Starting point of Jesus' Ascension
Place where a woman anointed Jesus' feet
Location on the eastern bank of the Jordan where John baptized
G0963.detail:
1. Bethany is a small village located fifteen stadia (about three kilometers) from Jerusalem, towards the Mount of Olives. It is a strategic location on the access roads to Jerusalem, which Jesus frequents during his visits to Judea (Matthew 21:17; Mark 11:1).
2. Bethany is the home of Lazarus, Mary, and Martha, where Jesus raises Lazarus after four days of death, one of his greatest miracles (John 11:1, 18).
3. It is also the place from which Jesus ascends to heaven after his resurrection, blessing his disciples before the Ascension (Luke 24:50).
4. A woman anoints Jesus with precious perfume in this house during the last days before his passion, an act that foreshadows his burial (Mark 14:3).
5. John also mentions a Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John the Baptist conducted his ministry, probably in the southern Jordan (John 1:28).
G0963.origine: The original Hebrew name, "Béith Aninèya," literally means "house of affliction" or according to another interpretation "house of dates" (evoking the agricultural abundance of the place). It is a compound place name, formed from "béith" (house) and a word designating either distress or a type of fruit or plant. The name has retained this Aramaic-Greek form in all the Gospels.
G0963.emploi: Bethany appears twelve times in the New Testament, exclusively in the four Gospels. It is a center of pastoral and family life: Jesus often goes there from Jerusalem to rest (Matthew 21:17), and he spends the night at his friends' house (John 12:1). The three main events associated with Bethany are the resurrection of Lazarus, the meal where Jesus is anointed, and the Ascension. John distinguishes two places of the same name: the one near Jerusalem and the one by the Jordan where John baptized (John 1:28), which shows the importance of the place in the biblical topography of the ministry of Jesus and John the Baptist.
G0963.portee: Bethany symbolizes hospitality and friendship: it is where Jesus finds rest, affection, and understanding before his passion. The resurrection of Lazarus demonstrates Jesus' power over death and his love for his friends, the foundation of the disciples' faith. The Ascension that departs from there makes this ordinary village the threshold of heaven. For the modern reader, Bethany reminds us that Jesus did not disdain simple family life and that humble places can become lands of miracle and revelation.

sens: pool in Jerusalem
place of miraculous healing
G0964.detail: 1. Bethesda is a pool (water basin) located in Jerusalem, near the Sheep Gate. Its name, in Hebrew or Aramaic, would literally mean "house of mercy" or "house of grace," which corresponds well to its function. 2. It is the place where Jesus heals a man who had been paralyzed for thirty-eight years: the sick man lies among other invalids waiting for the water to be stirred, believing that the first to enter will be healed. The pool symbolizes a place of hope and salvation, but also of doubt and human impotence until Jesus intervenes with his word of life.
