G0964.origine: The name Bethesda is a Hebrew or Aramaic word composed of "beth" (house) and "hesda" (mercy or grace). It evokes a place dedicated to divine compassion and the restoration of the sick. The exact etymology is debated among scholars, but the general meaning refers to divine goodness towards the suffering.
G0964.emploi: Bethesda appears only once in the New Testament, in John 5:2. John describes it as a pool with five porticoes (covered galleries) where many invalids, blind, lame, and paralyzed people gathered. It is there that Jesus meets the long-paralyzed man and heals him by commanding him to get up and carry his bed, performing a miracle on the Sabbath. This place becomes the setting for a major teaching on the power of the Son of God and his freedom concerning the law.
G0964.portee: Bethesda reminds the reader that Jesus heals not through rites or superstitious beliefs, but through his living word. The contrast between the sterile waiting of the sick and the direct intervention of Jesus shows that true salvation comes from Him alone, not from our efforts. This account invites every Christian to recognize their own infirmity and turn to Christ for true healing.

sens: City in Judea, located south of Jerusalem
Birthplace of Jesus
City of David, ancestral home of King David
G0965.detail:
1. Bethlehem is a small town located in Judea, about 9 kilometers south of Jerusalem. It is there that Joseph and Mary went for the census, and it is in Bethlehem that Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1; Luke 2:4).

2. According to the Gospels, Jesus was born in Bethlehem in fulfillment of the Old Testament prophecies that announced that the Messiah would be born in this city (Matthew 2:5-6; John 7:42). This central event of the Christian Christmas gives Bethlehem its major spiritual significance.

3. Bethlehem is also known as the "city of David" because it was the homeland of King David, the greatest king of Israel. Joseph and Mary went there precisely because Joseph was of the house of David (Luke 2:4).
G0965.origine: The Hebrew name Bethlehem literally means "house of bread" (beït = house, lehem = bread). This name evokes both the agricultural abundance of the region and, for Christians, Jesus who presents himself as the "bread of life." The name of the city already appears in the Old Testament as the birthplace of King David (1 Samuel 16).
G0965.emploi: Bethlehem appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in the nativity accounts of Matthew and Luke. In Matthew (2:1, 5, 6, 8, 16), it is at the heart of the narrative: it is where Jesus is born, where the Magi seek the king of the Jews, and where Herod orders the killing of the children to eliminate the newborn. In Luke (2:4, 15), Bethlehem is presented as the city of David, justifying that Jesus is born there. In John 7:42, it appears in a discussion about the identity of the Messiah: the crowd wonders if the Messiah really comes from Galilee, for "does not the Scripture say that the Messiah comes from the descendants of David and from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?"
G0965.portee: Bethlehem reminds Christians that Jesus, the King of kings, voluntarily incarnated himself in the humility of a small provincial town, far from the great centers of power. The very name, "house of bread," takes on Christian meaning: the one who is born in Bethlehem will become the bread of life for all believers. It is also a place where the prophetic word of the Old Testament is fulfilled, attesting that Jesus is indeed the promised Messiah.

sens: City on the northeast shore of the Sea of Galilee
G0966.detail: Bethsaida is a small town located on the northeast shore of the Sea of Galilee in Judea. Its name means in Aramaic "house of fish," indicating its role as a fishing port. It is from there that the apostles Peter, Andrew, and Philip came (John 1:44). Jesus healed a blind man there (Mark 8:22) and withdrew with his disciples to rest after a mission (Luke 9:10). Although little known today, this town was the site of several acts of Jesus reported in the Gospels.
G0966.origine: The name Bethsaida comes from the Aramaic: "beth" means "house" and "saida" means "fish." Thus, it literally means "house of fish." This name reflects the local economy based on fishing in the Sea of Galilee. The town was an important center of the disciples' life and Jesus' activity in Galilee.
G0966.emploi: Bethsaida appears 7 times in the Gospels. It is the homeland of three major apostles: Peter, Andrew, and Philip (John 1:44). Jesus visits it to heal a blind man (Mark 8:22), withdraws there with his disciples (Luke 9:10), and addresses it alongside Chorazin for the rebuke regarding the unbelief of its inhabitants despite the miracles performed (Matthew 11:21, Luke 10:13). These passages show that Bethsaida was a place of apostolic life and Jesus' ministry, despite the general resistance of its inhabitants to his message.
G0966.portee: Bethsaida reminds us that the Kingdom of God did not spare even the places closest to Jesus. Although three apostles came from there and Jesus performed miracles, the majority of the inhabitants refused to repent. This teaches the importance of responding to divine grace when it manifests, and the peril of unbelief even in the face of the clearest divine evidence.

sens: Village near Jerusalem, on the way to the Mount of Olives
G0967.detail: 1. Bethphage is a small village located on the outskirts of Jerusalem, on the road leading to the Mount of Olives. It is from there that Jesus sent two disciples to fetch the colt with which he would make his triumphant entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:1, Mark 11:1). The name literally means "house of unripe figs" in Aramaic, evoking a place planted with unripe fig trees — a very local and precise image of the Judean landscape. The three Synoptic Gospels mention this village as an important geographical landmark: it is there, at the border between the countryside and the holy city, that the final act of Jesus' ministry begins.
G0967.origine: The name comes from the Aramaic "bêt" (house) and "pagê" (unripe figs). It is a very specific place name, linked to the geography and flora of the Jerusalem region. The Evangelists retained it in its Aramaic form rather than translating it, which shows that they aimed for historical and geographical accuracy — they wanted the reader to precisely locate the place where the events took place.
G0967.emploi: Bethphage appears only three times in the New Testament, solely in the accounts of Jesus' triumphant entry into Jerusalem. Matthew, Mark, and Luke all mention it in a very similar way: it is the starting point of the episode where Jesus sends his disciples to fetch a colt to fulfill the prophetic Scriptures. The village is always associated with the Mount of Olives and is often mentioned alongside Bethany, the neighboring village where Jesus raised Lazarus. Bethphage is never the site of a major action in itself; it is a landmark, a waypoint marking the proximity of Jerusalem and the imminence of the climax of Jesus' earthly ministry.

sens: A step, a stride
A platform or pedestal
The seat of a magistrate or authority where justice is rendered
The tribunal of God or Christ for divine judgment
G0968.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply "a step" or "a stride": Abraham receives a land where he cannot even place his foot (Acts 7:5). This meaning comes from the verb that means to walk.
2. A platform or pedestal built with steps to ascend: it is an elevated platform from which one can be seen and heard.
3. By extension, the seat or tribunal of a Roman magistrate where justice is rendered: Pilate is seated on the tribunal (Matthew 27:19), Paul appears before that of the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:12) or before that of Caesar (Acts 25:10).
4. Applied to God and Christ, it designates the divine tribunal from which the final judgment emanates: we will all appear before the tribunal of God (Romans 14:10) or before that of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10).
G0968.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to walk." It first evokes the act of placing the foot on the ground, then the idea of ascending by degrees, hence the platform or pedestal. The Hebrew word it often translates in the Old Testament is one that means "footstool" or "pedestal." By its image of height and dominance, the tribunal embodies the authority of the one who sits.
G0968.emploi: The word appears twelve times, mostly in Acts and the Pauline epistles. In its concrete senses (step, platform), it is rarely found: Acts 7:5 speaks of placing the foot. The dominant sense is that of the seat of justice: Matthew, John, and Acts describe the tribunals of Roman authorities (Pilate, Gallio, Felix). Paul, as a prisoner, appears before these tribunals. Finally, Paul broadens the meaning to the divine tribunal: in Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10, we will all appear before the tribunal of God or Christ. The word thus takes on an ethical dimension: earthly justicer first, it becomes the symbol of eternal judgment.
G0968.portee: This word confronts the Christian with two truths. First, before human tribunals, only Christ or God does not deceive: one must seek justice from Him, not from the magistrates of the world. Secondly, Romans 14:10 reminds us that each will appear before the tribunal of God to account for their life. This is a call not to judge one's brother hastily, since we will all be judged. This word engraves moral responsibility in the heart of the reader.

sens: Precious stone of sea-green color
Material used in the ornaments of the temple
G0969.detail:
1. Beryl is a precious stone of a beautiful sea-green color. In Revelation, John lists the twelve stones that adorn the foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem, and beryl is the eighth among them (Revelation 21:20), symbolizing the beauty and purity of the New City.
2. This stone was known in the Old Testament as a precious material used in the ornaments of the temple and divine worship, showing that it had value in the eyes of God's people long before John mentioned it in his vision.
G0969.origine: The Greek word bērullos designates this well-known sea-green gem in the Mediterranean basin. It likely comes from an ancient Sanskrit word (vaidūrya) that circulated through trade routes to the Greeks. Beryl has been valued as an ornamental stone since antiquity, which explains its presence in descriptions of the temple and the City of God.
G0969.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John's vision in Revelation 21:20. This unique mention is part of the solemn description of the foundations of the New Jerusalem, where twelve precious stones of great beauty represent the glory of the Church of Christ. The context is that of a vision of heaven, where the stone embodies a part of divine magnificence.
G0969.portee: Beryl, like the other precious stones of the heavenly Jerusalem, reminds the believer that the perfection of the eternal City surpasses all earthly beauty. It is an invitation to set our sights not on the riches of the present world, but on the incomparable glory that God prepares for His own. This image encourages us to persevere in faith knowing that our eternal inheritance will be more precious than all the treasures of the world.

sens: Brutal force exerted against someone or something
Agitation or tumult of a crowd
Irresistible power of nature
G0970.detail:
1. Violence is a brutal force that is exerted against someone to master or control them against their will: this is what the commander in Jerusalem feared he would have to employ against Paul, fearing that the people would stone him (Acts 5:26). When the soldiers had to carry him up the steps, it was because the violence of the crowd was pressing in on him from all sides (Acts 21:35).
2. The word also refers to the brute force of an agitated and uncontrollable multitude that surges against someone: the tribune Lysias had to forcibly pull Paul from the hands of the Jews, that is, by using the coercive force of his soldiers to rescue him from the raging crowd (Acts 24:7).
3. Violence can also be that of natural forces, inhuman and overwhelming: it is the violence of the waves that broke the back of the ship during the shipwreck (Acts 27:41), a power against which men can do nothing.
G0970.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes strength and physical power. It denotes any form of brutal force or coercion imposed by strength. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew *perek* (oppression, cruelty), which carries the image of what crushes and subjugates.
G0970.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, all in the book of Acts and concerning Paul: twice to describe the violent agitation of a tumultuous crowd (5:26 and 21:35), once for the coercive action of the tribune who pulls him from the popular wrath (24:7), and once for the irresistible power of the waves that break a ship (27:41). In all cases, the word emphasizes the absence of gentleness or restraint: it is a force that acts without mercy, whether that of a raging crowd or that of nature.
G0970.portee: This word reminds us that brute force — that of the crowd, authority, or even nature — resolves nothing: it can only subjugate or destroy. For Paul, persecuted yet faithful, the violence of men changes nothing about his mission. For every Christian, it is a lesson: true power is not that of violence, but that of the Gospel.

sens: To constrain someone by force
To progress with impetuosity, with fervor
To appropriate something by force or ardor
G0971.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to constrain someone despite their resistance: one forces them to act against their will. It is a term of physical or moral violence. In Matthew 11:12, Jesus speaks of the kingdom of heaven that is "forced," meaning either conquered by force or violently pressed to advance.

2. The word also expresses the idea of progressing or advancing with great impetuosity, like someone who rushes forward with fervor. In Luke 16:16, it describes those who "use violence to enter" the kingdom: the image is that of a crowd pressing with force, striving to access it with intensity.

3. By extension, it means to seize something by force or ardor, as one conquers a territory or grabs a coveted prize. The word suggests both intense effort and the unilateral nature of the action: one takes without asking for permission.
G0971.origine: The word comes from the root βία (bia), which means "force, violence." The family also includes βιαίως (biaiōs, "violently") and βίαιος (biaios, "violent"). In Hebrew, it often translates the roots פרץ (paratz, "to break through, to burst forth") and פצר (patsar, "to insist strongly"), which evoke the idea of forcing or breaking through resistance. The word paints the image of a power that does not allow itself to be stopped.
G0971.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two key passages we have: Matthew 11:12 and Luke 16:16. In these two parallel verses, Jesus evokes the intense movement of the kingdom of God at the time of John the Baptist. The word is ambiguous: scholars debate whether it indicates a generous conquest (the disciples eagerly appropriating the kingdom) or fierce resistance (the enemies of the kingdom attempting to violate it). The context of each passage — the stakes of the kingdom and the spiritual urgency — shows that the word denotes a powerful, irresistible dynamic that characterizes the new era of salvation. The rarity of the word makes it a deliberately chosen term by Jesus to emphasize the intensity of the moment.
G0971.portee: These two verses invite the reader to understand that the kingdom of God is not entered passively: it requires fervor, personal commitment, a "violence" in the spiritual sense of a strong and determined intention. Jesus does not speak of soft gentleness, but of the power with which one must turn to God. The word also invites not to remain a spectator: the kingdom of God calls those who desire it to give themselves entirely, to "force" the doors of grace with confidence and perseverance.

sens: That occurs with force and suddenness
That sweeps away with violence
That acts or speaks with force and without restraint
G0972.detail:
1. Impetuous describes what happens with a sudden and irresistible power: the wind at Pentecost comes "from heaven" all at once, like a natural force that invades everything (Acts 2:2). The emphasis is on suddenness and intensity.
2. The word evokes a force that sweeps away, that subjugates everything in its path: an impetuous wind fills the entire house, and it cannot be restrained.
3. Figuratively, impetuous also applies to a person, a word, or an action carried out with fervor, without gentleness or restraint, with a power that ignores obstacles.
G0972.origine: The Greek word comes from the root βία (bia), which means "force, brute power." It is the corresponding adjective, expressing what is filled with or marked by this force. In Hebrew, this word often translates terms meaning "strong," "violent," or "harsh."
G0972.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 2:2, at the moment when the Holy Spirit descends on the disciples at Pentecost. It describes the sound "like that of a mighty wind" that fills the house. The context shows that this term serves to express the sudden, powerful, and irresistible nature of the divine intervention: it is not a gentle breeze, but a spectacular manifestation of God's power.
G0972.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate Pentecost not as a tranquil event, but as a major and sovereign irruption of the Holy Spirit. The impetuosity of the wind symbolizes the transformative power of God: it does not depend on our strengths; it seizes us and changes us. It is a reminder that the work of God is never weak or hesitant.

sens: who uses physical or moral force in a brutal and excessive manner
who acts with intense and irresistible fervor
G0973.detail:
1. The violent person is one who resorts to brute force, imposing their will through brutality. This is the primary meaning of the word in Greek: a person who does not shy away from coercion or aggression. In Matthew 11:12, Jesus speaks of the "violent" who "take hold of" the kingdom of heaven — not cruel men, but those who seize it with fierce determination, without hesitation or half-measures.
2. By extension, the word designates one who pursues a goal with intense and irresistible passion, without restraint. It is less about moral brutality than about unbridled fervor: the man who charges ahead, who does not yield, who takes hold of what he desires. In the context of the Kingdom, this becomes a spiritual quality: that of the believer who seeks it with burning zeal, a determination that knows no failure.
G0973.origine: The word comes from the verb βιάζω (biazo), "to use violence, to compel," itself derived from βία (bia), "force, violence." It is a family of words that speaks of brute power and constraint. The suffix -τής (-tēs) creates an agent noun: one who performs the action. The word is a late formation in Greek, but the image is ancient: the force that imposes itself, irresistible.
G0973.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 11:12. Jesus has just described John the Baptist and his preaching; he then says that "the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force." The context is that of the turning point brought about by John's preaching and the arrival of Jesus: a change so radical, so intense, that only those who have the fervor of the "violent" can seize it. The word thus carries a particular nuance: it does not speak of wickedness, but of passion, of a determination that refuses to let go. It is a portrait of the true disciple.
G0973.portee: For the Christian, this word invites reflection on the quality of their commitment to the Kingdom. Jesus does not call for soft gentleness or indifference: he praises those who pursue him with fervor, intensity, and uncompromising determination. It is a call to a living spiritual zeal, to refuse lukewarmness. This does not mean aggressiveness or harshness, but rather that heart-felt passion that seizes the Kingdom as an invaluable treasure and refuses to let it go.

sens: A small scroll or codex written, of reduced format
The book that the angel of the Apocalypse hands to John
The object of a mysterious spiritual experience: eating the written Word
G0974.detail:
1. The word designates a small book or written scroll, a reduced version of an ordinary book. It is a Greek diminutive that emphasizes the compact format: not a large register or an imposing scroll, but something that can be held in the hand and even, as the narrative indicates, swallowed. In Revelation 10:2, John sees an angel "holding in his hand a small open book."
2. This small book is the central object of the vision in chapter 10: the mighty angel descends from heaven with this small book in hand, and he commands John to take it and eat it. This is a symbolic act loaded with spiritual meaning, not simply a fanciful image. The angel says in Revelation 10:9: "Take it, and eat it."
3. By eating it, John experiences this small book in an intimate and embodied way: first sweet as honey in the mouth (Revelation 10:9), then bitter in the stomach (Revelation 10:10). This dual flavor expresses the ambiguity of receiving and integrating the Word of God: it is precious and pleasant, but it also brings a burden of difficult realities.
G0974.origine: The Greek word comes from Indo-European roots related to writing and paper (βίβλος means "book," from which we get our words "Bible" and "bibliotheca"). The diminutive suffix -άριον emphasizes the small format: it is a "little" biblia. This Greek diminutive has not been found elsewhere in known literature before the Apocalypse; John may have coined or adopted it to precisely express that this celestial scroll is compact, portable, and meant to be absorbed.
G0974.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Revelation 10 (verses 2, 9, and 10). John sees this angel descending from heaven holding this small open book; John asks him to give it to him; and John eats it. The narrative progresses from visual observation (v. 2) to action (v. 9-10). The small book is likely the complete divine revelation or a prophetic message that John must ingest for it to become part of himself so that he can then proclaim it. It is a biblical image of consuming the Word: eating and digesting the Word to live it and proclaim it.
G0974.portee: This image of the small book to eat teaches that receiving the Word of God is not just about reading or passively listening, but about internalizing it and allowing it to transform our lives. The contrast between sweetness and bitterness reminds us that the Word can be both comforting and demanding: it promises grace, but it also reveals realities that disturb the conscience. For the Christian, it is an invitation to not receive the Bible as a mere text, but as living food that must be digested and allowed to work in us.

sens: Written document on papyrus or parchment, a scroll intended to be read
Official act establishing a right or obligation
Complete account of the words and deeds of Jesus
Heavenly register where the names of the redeemed are inscribed
Prophetic text whose words must not be altered
G0975.detail:
1. A book in antiquity was a scroll of papyrus that one would unroll to read. Jesus himself "unrolled" the Law at home, as recounted in Luke 4:17, where he takes the scroll of the prophet Isaiah to read in the synagogue.
2. The word also designates a written legal document, notably the certificate of divorce: it is a "letter of divorce" that Moses allowed the husband to give to his wife (Matthew 19:7).
3. A book can also be the entirety of a person's acts and words — John notes that if all the miracles of Jesus were written "in detail," the world could not contain the books (John 21:25).
4. In Revelation, the book becomes symbolic: it is the book of life from Heaven, a divine register where the names of those who will inherit eternal life are inscribed (Revelation 21:27).
5. Finally, the prophetic book — that of the Apocalypse itself — has its words protected: neither add nor take away (Revelation 22:18-19), for it is the word of God recorded in writing.
G0975.origine: The Greek biblion is a diminutive of the word biblos (papyrus). It comes from the ancient practice where papyrus, the primary writing material, was rolled into scrolls. In the Old Testament, this word generally renders the Hebrew sepher, which means "that which is written" or "written document." The basic image is thus that of written papyrus: that which bears writing.
G0975.emploi: This word appears about 30 times in the New Testament, mostly in Revelation (more than half of the occurrences). It primarily designates the physical book — the scroll of the Law or the Prophets that Jesus reads publicly. It also takes on a legal sense: the act of divorce. But its major use is theological and eschatological: the book of life where God inscribes the names of the elect, and the book of prophecy given to John. The Apocalypse itself emphasizes this book as a sacred text that must not be violated (Revelation 22:10, 18-19). The context thus determines whether the word speaks of a material object or a heavenly reality.
G0975.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God entrusts his word in writing — first the Law and the Prophets, then the Gospel. It is a sign of the importance of the written Word. The book of life also shows that God keeps a record of those who belong to him: no name escapes him. Finally, Revelation warns: the Scriptures, once established, must not be altered — they stand as the word of God recorded.

sens: an object containing written text, scroll or codex
sacred or foundational document
heavenly register where the elect are inscribed
G0976.detail:
1. A physical object containing written text, most often a rolled scroll of papyrus (in ancient Greek, the word comes from Egyptian papyrus). Thus, in Mark 12:26, Jesus refers to the "book of Moses" as a written document containing the words of God — it is not merely a narrative, but a fixed text.
2. A sacred or foundational work that is respected and cited with authority, particularly the Hebrew Scriptures. In Luke 3:4 and Acts 7:42, it is "the book of the words of Isaiah" or "the book of the prophets": this refers to collections recognized as the word of God. This sense includes a nuance of veneration, as noted in the source definition.
3. A heavenly register, a role of those whom God recognizes as His own. In Philippians 4:3, Paul speaks of workers "whose names are in the book of life" — an image of divine election. Similarly, in Revelation 20:15, anyone whose name is not written in the "book of life" is thrown into the lake of fire: this book is the book of God's destinies, which determines who enters His kingdom.
G0976.origine: The word comes from the Greek βύβλος (byblos), which referred to Egyptian papyrus or the paper made from it. It is by metonymy — the material becoming the name of what is made from it — that the word came to mean a book or written document. In the Greek Old Testament (the ancient translation of the Hebrew Scriptures), βίβλος generally translates the Hebrew word סֶפֶר (sepher), which primarily means a written object, then a recognized work or collection.
G0976.emploi: The word βίβλος appears ten times in the New Testament, particularly in Luke and Acts. It is used much less frequently than its close relative βιβλίον (bibliôn), and with a more solemn connotation. In the Gospels and Acts, it almost always refers to the Hebrew Scriptures (Matthew 1:1 with "genealogy", Mark 12:26, Luke 3:4, Luke 20:42, Acts 1:20, Acts 7:42), documents recognized as the supreme authority. In Acts 19:19, the converts from Ephesus burn books of magic, showing that a book can be an object of spiritual influence to be destroyed. Finally, in Paul and Revelation (Philippians 4:3, Revelation 3:5, Revelation 20:15), the word takes on a more mystical meaning: the "book of life" where God inscribes the names of those who belong to Him. This evolution of meaning — from written document to heavenly register — reflects a theology where earthly writing points to God's eternal reality.
G0976.portee: For the believer, the word "book" reminds us that God's revelation is fixed, transmissible, and worthy of veneration. When Scripture is called a "book", it is not a passing opinion, but a recorded and stable word that can be quoted and deepened. The "book of life" in Revelation invites bold confidence: our salvation is not a chance occurrence or a fleeting wonder, but inscribed in God's eternal thoughts, where He recognizes us as His own.

sens: To consume food, to have a meal
G0977.detail: 1. To eat means to consume food for nourishment. In John 6:13, after the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves, the text reports that the disciples gathered the pieces "after everyone had eaten" — that is, after the crowd had consumed the bread and fish that Jesus had distributed.
G0977.origine: The verb βιβρώσκω (bibrōskō) is a poetic and later form of Greek. It belongs to the family of words expressing the action of eating and corresponds in Hebrew to אכל (akal), the most common verb for eating. This root is found in several Semitic and Indo-European languages, confirming the universality of the concept.
G0977.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in John 6:13. It is used in a historical and narrative context: describing the concrete action of the crowd that is being fed. The use of the verb in the past emphasizes that the action of eating is completed at the time of the narrative — it is after the meal that the leftovers were gathered.
G0977.portee: This verb underscores the material reality of the miracle: it is not merely a multiplication of numbers or symbols, but real food that truly satisfied the crowd. The fact that leftovers remained after everyone had eaten makes the miracle even more striking.

sens: Roman province located in the northwest of Asia Minor, by the Black Sea
G0978.detail: 1. Bithynia is a historical region in the northwest of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), bordered by the Black Sea. It was a prosperous Roman province with important cities. Paul and his companions sought to enter it during his second missionary journey, but the Spirit of Jesus prevented them, guiding them to Macedonia in Europe (Acts 16:7). Peter addresses his first epistle to Christians scattered in several provinces of Asia Minor, including Bithynia, indicating that a significant Christian community already existed in this region (1 Peter 1:1).
G0978.origine: The Greek name Bithunia designates this ancient province of the Mediterranean world. It is a toponym (place name) borrowed from the indigenous name of this historical region of the kingdom of Pergamum, which became a Roman province in 74 BC.
G0978.emploi: Bithynia appears twice in the New Testament, both in contexts of apostolic mission. During Paul's second journey (Acts 16:7), the Spirit prevents him from entering, redirecting the expansion of Christianity towards Europe. Later, Peter mentions Bithynia among the provinces where scattered Christians live, attesting that the Gospel had taken root there quickly despite Paul's initial refusal to go. These two passages show that Bithynia was a key region for the expansion of early Christianity in Asia Minor.

sens: The period or course of a person's life
The wealth, material goods necessary for living
What occupies or concerns daily life: worries, pleasures
G0979.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the duration and course of earthly existence: the life one lives, day after day. It is the biography of a person, their story. In 1 Timothy 2:2, we pray for a peaceful and quiet life, meaning a serene existence. In 2 Timothy 2:4, the soldier abstains from the affairs of civilian life, meaning he does not concern himself with ordinary daily activities.
2. The word also means material goods, what one possesses and what allows one to live. Luke 8:43 speaks of a woman who spent all her "wealth" on doctors: she consumed her resources. Luke 15:12 recounts how the father divides his "wealth" among his sons, meaning his properties and riches. Mark 12:44 and Luke 21:4 mention the offering of the widow who gives from her "necessities," all that she possessed to live.
3. The word can also encompass everything that absorbs life: worries, wealth, earthly pleasures. In Luke 8:14, the word of God is choked by the worries, riches, and pleasures of life. In 1 John 2:16, we are advised not to love the world nor "the lust of life" (the material desires that dominate existence).
G0979.origine: The word comes from a Greek root evoking the manner of living, the way of life. It is related to "bios" in modern French (biology = study of life, biography = story of a life). In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew "yamim" (days), as life is measured by its days. It is distinct from the Greek word "zôê" (ζωή), which means life in itself as a vital principle, while "bios" refers more to lived life, the concrete course of existence and what sustains it.
G0979.emploi: The word appears about a dozen times in the New Testament, especially in Luke and the epistles. In the Gospels (especially Luke), it designates material goods and sustenance: the wealth of the widow, that of a rich young man, or earthly food and worries. In 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, and 1 John, the meaning broadens: it can evoke the general course of existence (a peaceful life), or the desires and concerns that monopolize existence. The context often shows a tension between life dedicated to God and that absorbed by the goods or pleasures of the world. In 1 John 3:17, "bios" = having the resources, the necessities to help others.
G0979.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on what they truly consider their life. Is it the accumulation of goods and pleasures? Or an existence in service to God? The widow who gives from her necessities shows that authentic sacrifice consists of giving up what seems essential for physical life. For the disciple of Jesus, possessing true life (zôê eternal) often requires renouncing the concerns and riches that claim to occupy earthly life (bios). It is a call to prioritize: not to let the material choke the spiritual.

sens: To spend one's life, to make use of it
To live according to a given principle or will
G0980.detail:
1. To live means to spend one's life, to use the time given to us. It is more than existing: it is truly inhabiting the earth, making something of it. In 1 Peter 4:2, Peter speaks of the time left to live in the flesh — the time of our bodily existence before heaven.
2. To live can also mean to live according to a rule, a will. It is to live in a certain way, not just to exist. In 1 Peter 4:2, the apostle calls Christians to live now according to the will of God, and not according to human desires — it is a choice in how to lead one's life.
G0980.origine: The word comes from βίος (bios), which means life, existence — hence our French word "biography" (the account of a life). Βιόω is the verb formed from this noun. In the Greek translations of the Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word חיה (chaya), which means to live. It is a simple and direct word, without mystical nuance: it speaks of ordinary life, of time flowing.
G0980.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 4:2. Peter uses it to exhort persecuted Christians: while the world around them lives according to its own desires, they must use the rest of their earthly life to obey the will of God. The word emphasizes that life is a limited time, a space to fill, and it matters how one fills it. This is different from the verb ζάω (zao, see this word), which simply denotes the act of living or being alive, without emphasis on how it is used.
G0980.portee: This verb invites the Christian to reflect on the time they have left to live. It is not a life without end: it is a counted time, to be used intentionally. For the believer, this limit is not a threat, but an invitation not to waste their days following the desires of the world, but to fill them with obedience to God.

sens: The way one lives, their lifestyle, their conduct
The set of habits and choices that define an existence
G0981.detail:
1. The word designates the concrete manner in which someone lives daily: their habits, behavior, the way they conduct themselves. It is a person's lifestyle. Paul speaks of it in Acts 26:4 when he says that his "life" (in the sense of his conduct) from his youth is known to all the Jews, as he grew up in Jerusalem at the heart of his nation.
2. It can also evoke the entirety of the circumstances and choices that compose an existence — not only what one does, but where one lives, with whom, in what context. It is life as it unfolds in its concrete and observable details.
G0981.origine: The word comes from the verb to live (βιόω). It belongs to the same family as the words for "life" (βίος) and "living." In Greek, this term emphasizes not life itself, but the style, the manner, the form that life takes — hence the meaning of "way of life" or "lifestyle." It is a less common word in the New Testament, used mainly to emphasize how one leads their existence.
G0981.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 26:4. Paul uses it to describe his conduct since his youth: he reminds the Jews that his way of life is well known to them, as he grew up publicly among them in Jerusalem. By this term, Paul emphasizes that his life has not been hidden or secret — it has been lived before their eyes, observable, and thus his character as a pious Jewish religious figure was evident.
G0981.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that our way of life is a testimony: the way we conduct ourselves each day, our habits, our choices, is what makes our faith visible to others. Just as Paul calls the Jews to testify to his past conduct, we are called to live in a manner consistent with our faith, knowing that our life speaks before our words.

sens: Concerning the material needs and daily concerns of earthly life
Belonging to the realm of the temporal, as opposed to the spiritual
Related to earthly and transient matters
G0982.detail:
1. The word describes everything that touches on concrete and material life: eating, drinking, worrying about tomorrow, managing one's affairs. It encompasses the practical concerns that occupy people every day. In Luke 21:34, Jesus warns against the "overindulgence in eating and drinking, and the worries of life" — these material concerns that distract from what truly matters.
2. The word also designates what belongs to the visible and temporal world, distinct from spiritual and eternal realities. In 1 Corinthians 6:3, Paul reminds that believers will even judge angels, so it would be absurd for them not to judge "the matters of this life" — the minor material disputes among brothers. It is a gradation: if you can judge heavenly realities, why not earthly affairs?
G0982.origine: The word comes from the Greek "bios" which means "life" in the sense of living, concrete, and visible life (as opposed to "zôè," life as power). The suffix "-ikos" means "belonging to." Thus, "biôtikos" literally means "belonging to life" — that is, to life as it is lived day by day on earth, with its material necessities. It is an adjective formed to express what pertains to the realm of ordinary earthly existence.
G0982.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in Paul and in the words of Jesus in Luke. Each time, it contrasts with what transcends present life. In Luke 21:34, Jesus warns that the worries of life (food, drink, anxiety) can dull spiritual vigilance before His return. In 1 Corinthians 6:3-4, Paul uses it twice to show the relative insignificance of material disputes: believers are called to judge angels, so they should not entrust the judgment of simple everyday matters to unbelievers. The word always marks a distinction between the temporal and the eternal, the urgent and the essential.
G0982.portee: This word invites the Christian to a hierarchy of priorities. Material concerns are real and legitimate, but Jesus and Paul urge us not to become completely absorbed by them: what truly matters for the disciple is to remain vigilant before God and His promises. Understanding this distinction helps us keep worldly affairs in their proper place — useful, but not determinative for our spiritual destiny.

sens: Causing harm, damage
Seriously detrimental to moral or spiritual health
Gradually leading to ruin
G0983.detail:
1. The word designates what injures, damages, or harms. It is the adjective corresponding to the verb "to harm": something pernicious causes real harm, an injury. In 1 Timothy 6:9, Paul speaks of "pernicious desires" — cravings that wound the believer's soul.
2. More specifically, it refers to an evil that acts from within and gradually corrupts. The word evokes the image of poison or infection: it is not visible at first glance, but it insidiously destroys. The "foolish and pernicious desires" of 1 Timothy 6:9 are pernicious only because they gnaw at the believer's soul and plunge them into misery.
3. In a spiritual context, it means what leads to perdition. Paul directly links these desires to "ruin and destruction" — they lead a person toward their final destruction if they do not turn away from them.
G0983.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to strike, wound, harm." It is a regularly formed adjective: what has the capacity to harm is "harmful." The word family includes all terms related to the idea of damage or injury inflicted on someone or something.
G0983.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:9. Paul uses it to qualify the "foolish and pernicious desires" that tempt those who want to get rich. In this passage, the apostle shows that the pursuit of wealth is not innocent: it comes with desires that gnaw at the soul and lead to "temptation, a snare, and many foolish desires" — a spiral of spiritual destruction. It is a rare word, chosen intentionally to emphasize the seriousness of the danger.
G0983.portee: This term reminds the believer that some desires may seem like normal pleasures or ambitions, but they actually hide a logic of destruction. Wealth, success, power — things that are neutral in themselves — become "pernicious" when the heart becomes greedy. The text invites us to be vigilant about what attracts us: will it lead to our spiritual good or our ruin?

sens: To cause a wound, pain, or physical suffering to someone or something
To impair the integrity or health of a person
G0984.detail:
1. The word describes the action of injuring or causing someone to suffer physically. In Mark 16:18, Jesus assures that if believers drink a deadly poison, it will not harm them — in other words, no toxic substance will be able to damage them. It conveys the concrete idea of an attack on the body.
2. In a broader sense, it means to harm someone, putting their well-being or integrity at risk. In Luke 4:35, the demon leaves the possessed man without harming him: he frees him without further injuring him. The word thus encompasses any harm caused to a person.
G0984.origine: The Greek verb blaptō comes from an Indo-European root evoking the idea of striking or damaging. It belongs to a small family of Greek words related to damage and injury. In Greek, this verb is quite rare and classical; the translators of the Old Testament into Greek used it to render certain Hebrew terms meaning "to harm" or "to injure."
G0984.emploi: Blaptō appears only twice in the New Testament. Mark 16:18 and Luke 4:35 are our only attestations. The first passage speaks of material dangers (poison, snake bites) to which believers remain miraculously invulnerable. The second refers to the deliverance from demonic possession: the demon leaves its victim without inflicting further injuries. In both cases, the context is that of divine protection and the power of Jesus against the forces of evil.
G0984.portee: This word reminds us that faith in Jesus offers protection against forces that seek to harm us. It also emphasizes that divine deliverance is never brutal or harmful: it heals without injuring. For the reader, blaptō invites trust in God's ability to preserve us from evil, whether physical or spiritual.

sens: To germinate, to come out of the ground when speaking of a plant
To bloom, to be covered with flowers
To grow, to develop
To produce, to give birth (causative use)
G0985.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: a plant that pushes is a seed that germinates and comes out of the ground. In Matthew 13:26, the grass "pushes" (it grows), and then the tares also appear in the same field. This is the natural process of growth.

2. In Hebrews 9:4, it speaks of Aaron's rod that had "bloomed" — here the word specifically refers to the appearance and blossoming of flowers, a visible and magnificent sign.

3. In Mark 4:27, the seed "germinates" by itself, without the farmer understanding how. The sprout gradually rises from the soil; it is the first manifestation of the life hidden in the seed.

4. In James 5:18, the earth "produces" its fruit after the rain — here it is the causative use: the rain makes the earth grow, the rain is the cause that brings forth the fertility of the soil.
G0985.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes budding and germination. It often translates the Hebrew צמח (tsémakh, "sprout, shoot"), from which also comes the messianic title "the Sprout" applied to the Messiah in the Old Testament. The family of the word includes terms for the young shoot, the tender branch, the hatching of plant life.
G0985.emploi: The verb appears 4 times in the New Testament, mainly in parables and accounts of growth. Matthew and Mark use it to describe the growth of wheat and tares (natural germination), Hebrews for the miraculous blossoming of Aaron's rod (a sign of divine power), and James for the fertility of the earth after the rain (the visible effect of prayer). The meaning oscillates between the natural process of germination and the production of visible fruits, sometimes with a miraculous nuance.
G0985.portee: This word reminds us that spiritual growth, like the growth of plants, is a living process and often invisible at first. It also evokes the miracle: the dead rod of Aaron that comes back to life and blooms shows that only God can bring forth life. For the Christian, it is an invitation to let the word of God work in him, just as the seed grows without the farmer knowing how.

sens: An important figure at the court of King Herod Agrippa I
G0986.detail: 1. Blaste was the chamberlain of King Herod Agrippa I, meaning the trusted officer who managed the domestic affairs and access to the king. He is an influential man with the sovereign, as shown by the initiative of the Tyrians and Sidonians who win him over to their cause to obtain peace with the kingdom (Acts 12:20).
G0986.origine: The Greek name Blastos (Βλάστος) literally means "sprout" or "shoot," evoking the idea of growth. It is a common male name in ancient Greece, held here by a historical figure attached to the royal court of Herod Agrippa I.
G0986.emploi: Blaste appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 12:20, during an episode of tension between King Herod and the cities of Tyre and Sidon. These coastal cities depended on the wheat supply provided by the king's territory, and they had to seek reconciliation. The Tyrian and Sidonian envoys set a political trap by winning over Blaste, the influential chamberlain, which allowed them to access the king and negotiate peace.

sens: To speak impiously or contemptuously against God
To insult, to outrage someone with words
To discredit, to bring dishonor to the name or reputation of God
G0987.detail:
1. To blaspheme is to speak irreverently or contemptuously about sacred things, especially about God himself. It is to refuse to acknowledge his authority or holiness through words that offend him. For example, when the scribes hear Jesus forgiving sins, they think he is blaspheming, for only God can forgive (Matthew 9:3). It is the sin of doubting or denying divine rights and nature.
2. To blaspheme can also mean to insult or outrage someone with insults or contemptuous words. Those who crucify Jesus mock and curse him (Matthew 27:39). The word describes verbal attack, the personal affront thrown in someone's face.
3. To blaspheme against someone or against his name is also to ruin his reputation or honor. When one blasphemes the name of God among the Gentiles, one desacralizes it and obstructs his glory (Romans 2:24). Similarly, the bad conduct of servants causes the name of God to be blasphemed (1 Timothy 6:1). Blame diverts others from respecting what should be respected.
G0987.origine: The Greek word comes from the adjective "blasphemous" (βλάσφημος), which literally means "harmful" or "evil in speech." It associates the idea of word (φημή) with that of evil or misfortune. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb mainly translates Hebrew verbs meaning "to contradict," "to curse," or "to offend." The blame is always directed against what is sacred or against a person worthy of respect.
G0987.emploi: The verb "to blaspheme" appears 35 times in the New Testament and describes a wide range of transgressions. It can refer to insults against God: saying that Jesus blasphemes when he forgives sins (Matthew 9:3, Mark 2:7), or refusing him as the Son of God (John 10:36). It can target the Holy Spirit: whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit commits an unforgivable sin (Mark 3:29, Luke 12:10). It also applies to persecutions where Paul himself blasphemes against Christians (Acts 26:11) or to mockery against Jesus on the cross (Matthew 27:39). Finally, it describes the discredit thrown on the name and honor of God by the bad conduct of believers: the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles (Romans 2:24), or a wicked servant causes the divine name to be blasphemed (1 Timothy 6:1). The word thus covers both direct insult against God and indirect offense through failing testimony.
G0987.portee: Understanding blasphemy helps the believer measure the respect due to God and his name. The blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is presented as the only unforgivable sin: recognizing what this transgression consists of highlights the importance of the Spirit in salvation. For the disciple, this word reminds him that his daily conduct honors or dishonors the name of God in the eyes of the world: it is not only about avoiding impious words but also ensuring that his life brings glory to God rather than causing him to be blasphemed.

sens: injurious and contemptuous words directed at someone
slander, gossip, malicious insult
impious words against God, insult towards the Sacred
G0988.detail:
1. Blasphemy is primarily an injurious and contemptuous word, a discourse that seeks to belittle the one to whom it is addressed. It is the same root that produces the insult thrown lightly in a quarrel or dispute. In Ephesians 4:31, Paul asks that "all slander" disappear from among Christians, alongside anger and animosity: it is a sin of the mouth among others.
2. More specifically, blasphemy is a slander or gossip: a word that attacks the reputation of others, which willfully denigrates them. In Mark 7:22, it is listed among "thefts, covetousness, wickedness," as a vice that springs from an evil heart. It is the weapon of one who wants to destroy another's honor by words.
3. In its most serious sense, blasphemy is an impious word directed against God Himself or against the Sacred. At Jesus' trial, in Matthew 26:65, the high priest cries out, "He has blasphemed!" because Jesus declared Himself the Son of God: it is an outrage against the divine. In Revelation 13:5, the Beast "uttered blasphemies against God." It is the quintessential spiritual sin.
G0988.origine: The word comes from "blasphēmos," composed of a root meaning "to strike" or "to hit" and "phēmē" (the word). The initial image is that of a word that "strikes" or "wounds": the violent and destructive word. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the same concept is expressed by terms like "naatsah" (to despise, to mock): these are the words of the insolent who mock God or His people.
G0988.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. Matthew and Mark speak of it during the Passion: when Jesus is accused of blasphemy (Matthew 26:65, Mark 14:64), and when Jesus states the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, the unforgivable sin (Matthew 12:31, Mark 3:28). In Luke 5:21, the Pharisees see in the forgiveness of sins a blasphemy against God alone. Paul uses it in his lists of vices that must disappear from the believer's life (Ephesians 4:31, Colossians 3:8, 1 Timothy 6:4), where it rather means slander or insult. Revelation speaks of the blasphemies of the Beast and the accusers of the saints, giving the word all its spiritual weight of hostility towards God and His kingdom.
G0988.portee: For the Christian, blasphemy is a warning about the danger of unbridled speech. Jesus teaches that words reveal the heart (Matthew 15:19): what we say shows who we are. Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit marks the limit that God does not forgive — not out of a lack of grace, but because deliberately hardening oneself against the Spirit is to close oneself off to all forgiveness. In daily life, calling the believer to flee from slander, insult, and gossip reminds them that their mouth must honor God and others, never wound them.

sens: One who utters words against God, against holy things, or against others
Impious, sacrilegious, or insulting words towards God and His law
Injurious or contemptuous speech towards someone or something sacred
G0989.detail:
1. In its primary sense, a blasphemer is a person who utters offensive, contemptuous, or impious words directed against God, His ministers, or what He has established. In Acts 6:13, the false witnesses accuse Stephen of uttering "words against the holy place and against the law," that is, words that attack or belittle what God has ordained. Paul himself acknowledges having been a "blasphemer" in 1 Timothy 1:13, as he persecuted the disciples of Christ.
2. The word also designates the attitude of one who speaks ill, insults, or slanders. In 2 Timothy 3:2, the "blasphemers" of the last days are listed among men of perverse morals — selfish and ungrateful. Here, blasphemy is not just an offense against God: it is a trait of a vicious character, a tendency to slander and insult.
3. By extension, the term designates injurious or irreverent words towards any authority or creature of God. In 2 Peter 2:11, the angels "do not bring against them a railing judgment," meaning they refuse to utter words of contempt, even towards evil powers, maintaining the respect that is due to their dignity.
G0989.origine: The Greek word is composed of "blas-" (an obscure root, according to ancient scholars) and "phēmē" (word, speech). It literally means "bad word" or "word against." The Hebrew word it often translates in the Greek Old Testament is a form of the verb bârak (to bless) used in the opposite sense (to curse or insult). The root evokes the action of pronouncing — verbally — something violent and destructive against what deserves respect.
G0989.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts and Paul's epistles. In Acts 6:11, it qualifies the "blasphemous words" falsely attributed to Stephen before the Sanhedrin. Paul, in 1 Timothy 1:13, uses the noun to confess that he himself was a "blasphemer" before his conversion, linking this sin to persecution and violence. In 2 Timothy 3:2, it appears in the list of vices of the last days, characterizing depraved men who forget all fear of God. In 2 Peter 2:11, the adjective applies to "railing judgments," showing that blasphemy is not only a word against God, but any contemptuous or disrespectful word. The usage thus varies between the specific sin of insulting God and the broader moral vice of slander or insolence.
G0989.portee: This word reminds the Christian that speech has a fearsome power: insulting God, His servants, or His work is a serious transgression. Paul testifies to this by confessing his past as a blasphemer — but he also emphasizes that he received mercy, which encourages repentance. The term also warns that blasphemy is not isolated: it accompanies selfishness, ingratitude, and impiety. Finally, the example of the angels who even refuse injurious words invites the believer to a guarded, respectful, and kind speech.

sens: the action of looking, seeing
the way of seeing, vision
what one perceives with the eyes
G0990.detail:
1. Sight is primarily the simple action of seeing, of turning the eyes towards something. In 2 Peter 2:8, Lot "tormented his righteous soul" by what he saw — his sight of the criminal works of Sodom caused him inner suffering.
2. More broadly, this word designates the particular way in which one sees things, the visual impression one receives. This is why the Bible can speak of "sight" as a moral faculty: what we look at shapes our soul.
3. Sight can also mean what falls under our eyes, the spectacles or realities that we perceive. For Lot, it was the spectacle of the sins of his contemporaries.
G0990.origine: The word comes from the verb βλέπω ("to see, to look"), which is a fundamental root for vision in the Greek of the New Testament. Its initial image is simply that of the eye turning towards an object. The Bible often uses this verb and its derivatives to speak not only of physical vision but also of moral and spiritual perception — "to see" also means "to understand" or "to witness."
G0990.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:8. Peter uses it to describe how Lot, righteous in the midst of Sodom, was tormented by what he saw and heard of the criminal works around him. This unique occurrence shows that "sight" here designates the concrete visual perception — the spectacle of sins — which acts as a source of moral suffering for one who has a righteous conscience. The association of "sight" and "hearing" emphasizes that it is through his senses that Lot became aware of the surrounding iniquity.
G0990.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on the power of sight: what we see shapes our soul and conscience. Like Lot, the believer can be saddened or troubled by the spectacle of evil around him — this is not a weakness, but a sign of a righteous soul. It also calls us to be vigilant about what we look at, knowing that our moral vision depends on what we focus our attention on.

sens: Perceive with the eyes, have the ability to see
Look at something or someone in a particular way
Discern, perceive with the intellect or heart
Pay attention to, take care, consider
Turn towards, look in the direction of
G0991.detail:
1. It is primarily physical vision: having functioning eyes and perceiving what is in front of oneself. The blind cannot see, but one who regains sight can (John 9:7: "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam. So he went, washed, and came back seeing"). This is the simplest and most direct meaning of the word.

2. To look means to fix one's attention on something specific: one sees deliberately, one sets one's gaze. Jesus notices the crowd pressing around him (Mark 5:31: "You see the crowd pressing against you"), or one sees the burning coals on the shore (John 21:9).

3. In the sense of the spirit or heart, to see is to understand, to perceive a hidden truth. The disciples are blessed to see what many prophets desired to see (Luke 10:23-24), for they are witnesses to the acts of Jesus. This is a deeper knowledge than mere sight with the eyes.

4. Paying attention is a call to vigilance: "Consider, brothers, that among you who are called there are not many wise" (1 Corinthians 1:26). The word then carries the meaning of "take care," "observe this."

5. Looking towards is the orientation of the gaze towards a direction or a person: when one looks someone in the face to judge them (Matthew 22:16: speaking of observing without regard to the person).
G0991.origine: The Greek verb βλέπω comes from a root that describes the action of turning the eyes towards something. In Hebrew, the word ראה (ra'ah) expresses the same concept: to see physically or to perceive intellectually. This root gradually enriches the meaning of "to observe" and "to become aware," reflecting the movement of the gaze inward, from the eye to the mind.
G0991.emploi: The verb βλέπω appears about 120 times in the New Testament, distributed across the four Gospels, Acts, and the epistles. In the Gospel of John, it dominates the discourse on the spiritual meaning of seeing: to see Jesus is to believe. In Mark and Matthew, the verb emphasizes both physical perception and the spiritual blindness of the disciples. In Acts, it is more factual: reporting what one has seen. In Corinthians and Hebrews, Paul uses the verb to exhort to spiritual vigilance and moral clarity: "Consider, brothers" (1 Corinthians 1:26) or "Take care against deception" (Colossians 2:8). The meaning thus shifts from the visible to the vigilant, from the observed to the spiritual reflex.
G0991.portee: Seeing is a biblical invitation on two levels. First, one must have their eyes opened to the realities around them: to the presence of Jesus, to his signs, to his compassion. Secondly, to see spiritually requires a conversion of the heart: the Pharisee looks but does not truly see, while the disciple sees by faith. For the Christian, this entry reminds that the Christian vision is primarily an act of faith in Jesus Christ who incarnates, reveals himself, and from which moral vigilance naturally follows.

sens: What must be placed or poured somewhere
What must be done, imposed by necessity or appropriateness
G0992.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of placing or pouring something, here the new wine into wineskins: it is the concrete idea of putting in place. In Mark 2:22 and Luke 5:38, Jesus speaks of the wine that must be put into new wineskins, for the old ones could not contain it.
2. More broadly, it refers to what must necessarily be done, what wisdom or logic imposes. The new wine requires new wineskins: it is a necessity, not a choice.
G0992.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb βάλλω (bállô), which means "to throw, to cast, to place." The form βλητέος expresses what must be done, what is necessary — an obligation arising from the nature of things. It is a verbal form that indicates a natural or logical necessity, like saying "what must be thrown away."
G0992.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the same passage reported by Mark and Luke. Both evangelists use it to explain Jesus' teaching on the wineskins: the new wine must be poured into new wineskins, for the old ones are too fragile. The context is that of the parable of the new wine and the old wineskins, where Jesus announces that his new message cannot adapt to the old forms of religion. The word thus expresses a practical and symbolic necessity.
G0992.portee: This word of Jesus reminds the reader that the Gospel brings something radically new, which does not fit with the old religious structures. The new wine requires new wineskins: it is an invitation to welcome the transformation that Christ brings, rather than trying to contain it within old frameworks. This speaks to those who hesitate between the old and the new covenant.

sens: Nickname given by Jesus to James and John, sons of Zebedee
G0993.detail: Boanerges is the nickname that Jesus gave to James and John, the two sons of Zebedee. This word literally means "sons of thunder" in Aramaic (the language Jesus spoke). The nickname likely evokes the fiery and passionate temperament of these two brothers, their fervor, or perhaps their way of speaking with strength and authority, like the thunder that rumbles and strikes.
G0993.origine: The word comes from Aramaic and is composed of two elements: bar ("son") and ergés ("thunder"). It is one of the few words of Jesus reported in Aramaic by Mark. By giving nicknames, Jesus followed a common practice among rabbis to express the character or spiritual role of his disciples.
G0993.emploi: This nickname appears only once in the Bible, in Mark 3:17, at the moment when Jesus calls his twelve apostles. Mark notes that Jesus called James and John "Boanerges" (sons of thunder). No other Gospel mentions this nickname. The Gospel of Mark reports it in Aramaic and explains it immediately, which shows the importance that the first Christian testimony gives to this authentic word of Jesus in his own language.
G0993.portee: This nickname shows us that Jesus saw in James and John not only their present flaws but also their future potential as disciples. The calling of a name often prophesies the spiritual path: these "sons of thunder" will become pillars of the Church (Galatians 2:9), whose words will resonate powerfully in the proclamation of the Gospel. It is an encouragement to see that Jesus transforms our character traits, even our natural impulses, to make them instruments of his Kingdom.

sens: To utter a loud call or exclamation that comes from the mouth with force
To call for help, to implore someone by shouting
To protest, to exclaim with passion or urgency
To shout towards someone, to address them
G0994.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a raw cry, a sound that bursts forth: it is John the Baptist who "cries" in the wilderness (Matthew 3:3), not whispering but raising his voice so that his message is heard. It is also Jesus dying who "cries out" with a loud voice (Mark 15:34), expressing through this cry the depth of his distress.

2. Crying out for help means making one's urgent need heard: the father of the only son "cries out" to Jesus (Luke 9:38) so that the Master will look at him and come to the aid of his child. It is a prayer uttered with force, a plea that demands an immediate response.

3. To cry can also mean to protest, to express indignation: unclean spirits let out loud cries as they leave the demon-possessed (Acts 8:7), thus expressing their fury or fear.

4. The cry can be a direct address: the blind man "cries out" to Jesus, Son of David (Luke 18:38), not to disturb but to attract his attention and ask for mercy. The nuance: the cry carries a vivid emotion — joy, distress, urgency — that distinguishes this verb from the simple "to call."
G0994.origine: The verb βοάω comes from the noun βοή (boē), which denotes a cry, the sound of a raised voice. This root corresponds in Greek to several Hebrew verbs of calling or crying — זעק (zakaq, "to cry") or קרא (kara, "to call") — especially when the Old Testament is translated into Greek. The word carries the idea of a voice that comes forth with force, like a call that must cross a distance or break through a barrier.
G0994.emploi: The verb βοάω appears twelve times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It describes the cry of John the Baptist announcing the Messiah, the cries of distress from the sick imploring Jesus, the acclamations or protests of the crowds. Its usage varies slightly: to cry alone (absolute), or to cry towards someone (with the dative: to cry to someone, upon someone). In Mark and Matthew, Jesus "cries out" on the cross, expressing the word that reveals his abandonment. In Luke, the supplicants "cry out" to Jesus to be helped. In Galatians 4:27, Paul quotes Isaiah speaking of joy that "cries out." It is a verb of strong emotion: it always implies an affect that drives one to raise their voice.
G0994.portee: Understanding this verb helps the reader to feel the urgency and emotional weight of the Gospel narratives. When someone "cries out" to Jesus, it is not a polite request: it is a heartfelt call, born of distress or faith. And when John the Baptist "cries" in the wilderness, his message is heard, it pierces — it is a word that seeks to awaken. Recognizing the biblical cry means hearing the voices of men and women turning to God with their true urgency.

sens: A loud noise made by the human voice, particularly an exclamation of call or distress
A vehement protest, a complaint that demands justice
G0995.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a cry in the physical sense: a voice that rises with force. In James 5:4, it is the cry of withheld wages that "cries out" — a vivid image where the injustice itself seems to make its voice heard, as if the stolen thing cries for vengeance to heaven.
2. More broadly, it is a vehement protest, a complaint that rises to God. The text speaks of the "cries of the harvesters," meaning their passionate protests against exploitation: these cries do not disappear into silence, but "reach the ears of the Lord of hosts." It is the cry of a victim calling for divine justice.
G0995.origine: The word βοή comes from a root that evokes noise, the sound of the voice. In Hebrew, it often translates זְעָקָה (zeʿâqâh), which has the same meaning: a cry that rises, a voice that cries for help or in protest. It is a vivid, very concrete word that paints the image of a voice that carries, that cannot be ignored.
G0995.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 5:4. In this passage, the apostle denounces the rich who withhold the wages of workers: it is a cry of prophetic denunciation. The context shows that this cry is addressed to God — the cries of the victims rise to his ears. It is a cry that demands a response, that calls for divine justice upon earthly injustice.
G0995.portee: This word teaches us that God hears. The complaints of those suffering from injustice — the exploited, the dispossessed, the humiliated — never remain silent to the ears of the Lord. Even when the world ignores the victims, God hears them. It is a word of comfort for those who cry in affliction, and a warning for those who silence justice through violence or malice.

sens: Assistance provided to someone in need or danger
Divine support or spiritual assistance
Device or technique to reinforce or maintain something
G0996.detail:
1. Help is the concrete assistance given to someone in difficulty. On the storm-tossed ship (Acts 27:17), the sailors use "helps" — cables or straps — to reinforce the hull and prevent it from breaking apart under the violence of the sea.
2. In a spiritual sense, help refers to the assistance that God provides to those who cry out to him. In Hebrews 4:16, the believer can "receive help in their needs" by approaching the throne of grace with confidence: God intervenes to support those who suffer or who are weak.
3. The word also encompasses any device, resource, or means deployed to hold firm in the face of threat. This is the technical sense of the nautical term: to reinforce, maintain, support.
G0996.origine: The word comes from the verb βοηθέω (boēthéō), which literally means "to run to the aid of" or "to come to help." The root evokes the image of someone rushing to assist. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew עֵזֶר (ézer), which denotes help, assistance, and particularly the "help" that God provides to his people.
G0996.emploi: The word βοήθεια appears twice in the New Testament. In Hebrews 4:16, it speaks of spiritual help — the grace and mercy that the believer obtains by approaching God. In Acts 27:17, it refers to material, concrete means: the cables used to brace and reinforce a ship shaken by the storm. This dual usage — both spiritual and technical — shows that the word denotes any type of help or support, whether divine or human, intangible or tangible. The context of the shipwreck in Acts emphasizes the urgency and gravity of the need.
G0996.portee: This word reminds the Christian that they are never left to themselves. In the face of sin, fear, or weakness, they can approach God with confidence to find the help they need (Hebrews 4:16). It is a word of comfort and hope: God is accessible, and his help is real and immediate for those who seek it.

sens: To come to the aid of someone in difficulty
To respond to a call for help
To provide support in a trial
To intervene to save or protect
G0997.detail:
1. To rescue primarily means to come to the aid of a person in danger or distress: to run towards them to help. The Canaanite woman cries out to Jesus, "Lord, help me!" (Matthew 15:25) because she needs His urgent intervention. It is an immediate and concrete action.
2. The word can also refer to the call for help itself, the cry by which one asks for assistance. In Jerusalem, the crowd cries out, "Help!" to alert about the presence of Paul (Acts 21:28). Here, it is less about the action than the call that matters.
3. To rescue is used to denote the moral or spiritual support provided to someone who doubts or suffers. The father of the young boy possessed cries out, "Help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24): he asks Jesus to strengthen him in faith.
4. Finally, to rescue expresses divine help: God "rescues" (protects and supports) those who call upon Him. The Lord says He rescues on the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), meaning He acts to save.
G0997.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: "boè" (the cry) and "theo" (to run). The basic image is that of someone running towards the cry — someone who rushes to the sound and cry of the one calling for help. It is an energetic word that evokes both urgency (the cry) and quick reaction (the running). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the closest word is "azer" (to help, to support), which reflects the same idea found in all the Greek passages.
G0997.emploi: The verb "to rescue" appears about 8 times in the New Testament, primarily to describe the help given to someone in physical or moral distress. Matthew and Mark use it in scenes of miracles or supplication: a woman, a father, a sick child implore Jesus' help. Acts uses it for urgent calls or mission requests (Paul and his Macedonian call in Acts 16:9). Paul uses the word for God's promise to rescue in the time of salvation. Hebrews and Revelation use it to express divine help or heavenly intervention. The meaning remains constant: to intervene quickly and effectively for the one who cries out.
G0997.portee: This word reminds the believer that they are never alone in their trials. Jesus has shown Himself attentive to the cries of those who plead with Him; He does not turn away those who implore Him. It is also an invitation to pray without fear and to believe that God responds to the cries for help from His children. The word awakens trust: God is the one who rushes, who listens, who intervenes.

sens: one who comes to the aid of someone in need
one who provides assistance or support
G0998.detail:
1. A helper is someone who comes to aid when needed, who is useful in difficulty. The psalmist affirms: "The Lord is my helper" (Hebrews 13:6), meaning he can count on God to support and protect him against threats and dangers.
2. More broadly, a helper is a person who provides assistance or support in an action or endeavor. It is someone you can count on, who is ready to intervene.
G0998.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb βοηθέω ("to run to the aid of"), formed from βοή ("cry") and θέω ("to run"): literally, one who runs towards the cry of alarm, who rushes when called. In Hebrew, this often corresponds to עזר ("to help, to support"). The word expresses the idea of someone who does not remain passive but actively intervenes.
G0998.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 13:6, where the psalmist confesses that the Lord is his helper. Here, "helper" refers to God Himself as the one who comes to the aid of the believer in the face of fear and human threats. The context emphasizes the assurance that the believer can have thanks to this divine help.
G0998.portee: This word reminds the Christian that they are never alone or abandoned: God is present as an active and faithful helper. It invites one to place their trust not in the strength or goodwill of men, but in God alone, who is capable of supporting us in every circumstance.

sens: A hole dug in the ground, deep and open
A cavity where one can fall and get lost
Figuratively: moral or spiritual wandering
G0999.detail:
1. A pit is a hole dug in the earth, deep enough for one to fall into and unable to get out alone. It is literally a trap: in Matthew 12:11, it is asked whether it is lawful to pull a sheep out of a pit on the Sabbath.

2. The word evokes the danger of falling and loss. One who falls into a pit needs to be rescued, like that sheep.

3. Jesus uses the image of the pit to speak of spiritual wandering. In Matthew 15:14 and Luke 6:39, a blind man leading another: both fall into a pit. Here, the pit represents error, false doctrine, and distance from the truth. One who does not see spiritually (the blind man) leads those who follow him into ruin.
G0999.origine: The Greek word bothunos originally designates a natural or dug cavity in the earth. It is a common word in ancient Greek to speak of pits, wells, or chasms. It translates the Hebrew פַּחַת (pakhath), which has the same concrete meaning: a hole, a pit, a trap. The image of the pit, the hole one falls into, carries with it the idea of danger, loss, and helplessness.
G0999.emploi: The word appears three times in the Gospels, only in Matthew and Luke, and always in relation to literal or figurative pits. In Matthew 12:11, the pit is concrete: it is an agricultural trap where a sheep can fall. In Matthew 15:14 and Luke 6:39, Jesus takes up the image proverbially to teach that the blind (those who ignore divine truth) cannot lead other blind people without leading everyone to fall. The idea progresses from the concrete to the spiritual: the pit becomes the symbol of wandering and condemnation.
G0999.portee: This image of the pit reminds disciples that it is dangerous to be guided by someone who lacks spiritual light, and more seriously, to follow false doctrines or spiritually blind teachers. It also invites discernment about who can truly teach and lead us in the ways of God. It is a call to spiritual vigilance and discernment.
